periods.title: Prehistoric Age
periods.tagline: Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic → Chalcolithic
periods.overview: Prehistory is defined in the source material as the period before the invention of writing in India, i.e. before c. 3000 BCE. It is classified by tools, technology and way of life into the Stone Age (Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic) and the Metal Age (Chalcolithic).

phases.name: Palaeolithic Age (Old Stone Age)
points: Oldest and longest phase
People lived in caves, rock shelters and open sites
Nomadic life; hunting & food gathering
No agriculture or pottery
Use of rough stone tools
Sub-phases: Lower, Middle, Upper Palaeolithic (Handaxe Culture)

phases.name: Mesolithic Age (Middle Stone Age)
points: Transitional phase; semi-nomadic life
Rock shelter and cave dwellings
Hunting, fishing & food gathering
Domestication of dog
Use of microlithic tools (arrowheads, knives, sickles)

phases.name: Neolithic Age (New Stone Age)
points: Food-producing stage begins
Agriculture (wheat, barley, rice in some regions)
Domestication of animals (cattle, sheep, goat)
Settled life – villages; pottery making
Polished stone tools – axes, adzes, celts, grinding stones

phases.name: Chalcolithic Age (Copper Stone Age)
points: Use of copper along with stone
Advanced agriculture; permanent settlements
Pottery with designs; trade & exchange
Development of early villages, later leading to urbanization

Neolithic: Mehrgarh (Balochistan) – earliest Neolithic site in South Asia

events.title: Palaeolithic Age begins
events.desc: Oldest phase of human presence in India; hunting and gathering, use of rough stone tools, cave and rock-shelter dwellings.

events.title: Mesolithic Age begins
events.desc: Transitional semi-nomadic phase; microlithic tools, domestication of the dog, elaborate rock paintings and burial practices (Sarai Nahar Rai).

events.title: Neolithic Age begins
events.desc: Beginning of agriculture and animal domestication; settled village life and pottery-making commence.

events.title: Chalcolithic Age begins
events.desc: Copper used alongside stone; painted pottery, trade networks and early villages that lead toward urbanization.

prelims: Order of Ages: Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic → Chalcolithic
Mehrgarh – earliest Neolithic site in South Asia
Bhimbetka – rock paintings
mains: Way-of-life transition across the four ages (nomadic → semi-nomadic → settled village → settled village + trade)
Regional distribution of prehistoric sites across North, Central, West, South India

quickFacts: Rough stone → Microliths → Polished stone → Copper + stone
Early Historic Age (with writing), from c. 1000 BCE onwards

periods.title: Indus Valley Civilization
periods.tagline: One of the world's earliest urban civilizations
periods.overview: The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization develops through four phases — Early, Mature, Late and Post Harappan — from early agricultural regionalization to a peak urban civilization with planned cities, standardized weights, and extensive trade, followed by decline and ruralization.

phases.name: Early Harappan (Regionalization Phase)
points: Emergence of early agricultural settlements
Rural villages, basic crafts
Development of regional cultures
Neolithic & Chalcolithic cultures in NW India
Mehrgarh as earliest site

phases.name: Mature Harappan (Urban Phase)
points: Growth of large towns; planned cities (grid pattern)
Script, seals, standardized weights
Long-distance trade; urban civilization at its peak
Great Bath, Granaries; drainage & sanitation system
Craft specialization (bead making, metallurgy, pottery)

phases.name: Late Harappan (Transition Phase)
points: Decline of urban centres; smaller settlements
Regionalization; change in material culture
Change in pottery (Black-on-red ware); shift in trade routes
Decrease in craft specialization
Cultural diffusion to Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Gujarat, Deccan

phases.name: Post Harappan (Late Phase)
points: Ruralization continues
Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture in some regions
Eastern and Deccan contacts
Gradual integration with Iron Age cultures

Economy: Agriculture: wheat, barley, pulses, sesame, cotton
Animal husbandry: cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, pig
Crafts: bead making, pottery, shell objects, metallurgy
Trade: Maritime trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha), Oman, Bahrain
Script & Language: Found on seals, tablets, pottery, copper objects
Short inscriptions (5–6 signs average); written right to left

sites.features: First site discovered (1921); granary, cemetery, seals
Most famous site; Great Bath, Great Granary, drainage system
Unique water management system; reservoirs; well-planned city
One of the largest sites; Mature Harappan culture

decline: Climatic Change – decreased rainfall, prolonged drought
Change in River Courses – shift in Ghaggar-Hakra (Saraswati) and other rivers
Floods – repetitive floods may have destroyed settlements
Depletion of Natural Resources – deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion
Invasion Theory – disproved; not supported by evidence
Internal Factors – over-urbanization, trade decline, economic crisis, social changes

events.title: Early Harappan phase begins
events.desc: Regionalization phase; emergence of early agricultural settlements and regional cultures in NW India.

events.title: Mature Harappan urban phase
events.desc: Growth of large planned towns with grid-pattern streets, standardized weights and measures, and extensive trade with Mesopotamia.

events.title: Late Harappan decline begins
events.desc: Decline of urban centres, smaller villages, changing pottery styles and shifting trade routes.

events.title: Post Harappan / ruralization
events.desc: Painted Grey Ware culture appears in some regions; gradual integration with Iron Age cultures.

prelims: Part of Ancient India (Prehistoric/Protohistoric); frequently asked on sites & features
Map-based questions (Sites & Rivers)
Standardized weights follow a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 160...)
mains: Important for GS Paper I – Ancient History
Art & Culture linkages (Seals, Script, Religion)
Theories of decline of the civilization

quickFacts: Mother Goddess worship; Pashupati (proto-Shiva) seal; sacred animals (bull, tiger, elephant, rhinoceros)
Well-organized society; no evidence of kings, palaces or large temples

periods.title: The Vedic Age
periods.tagline: Religious – Social – Political – Economic – Literary – Cultural Development, including the Contribution of Women
periods.overview: The Vedic Age moves through five stages — Early Vedic, Later Vedic, Late Vedic, Upanishadic, and the Transition to the Mahajanapada Age — covering the shift from tribal pastoral society in the Sapta-Sindhu region to settled agrarian, increasingly urban, philosophically reflective society across the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.

phases.name: Early Vedic Age
points: Sapta-Sindhu region (Punjab, NW India, parts of Afghanistan)
Composed the Rigveda
Semi-nomadic pastoral life; tribal chiefdoms (Jan, Vish, Gram)
Nature worship (Indra, Agni, Varuna)
Women participated in assemblies; composers of hymns (Lopamudra, Apala, Ghosha, Vishvavara)

phases.name: Later Vedic Age
points: From Sapta-Sindhu to Ganga-Yamuna Doab
Composed Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda, Brahmanas, Aranyakas
Permanent villages; agriculture begins; Varna system (flexible), Ashrama system begins
Janapadas emerge; kingship (Rajan) more hereditary
Women received education; Gargi, Maitreyi as philosophers

phases.name: Vedic Late Period
points: Eastern Ganga plains (Magadha, Kosala, Videha)
Rise of Mahajanapadas; growth of cities & trade
Development of iron technology
Varna system rigidifies; questioning of rituals begins
16 Mahajanapadas emerge (Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa)

phases.name: Upanishadic Period
points: Mainly in eastern India (Ganga-Yamuna Doab to Bihar)
Composed major Upanishads; philosophical inquiry into Brahman, Atman, Moksha
Rise of renunciation tradition; Guru-Shishya tradition strengthened
Prominent women philosophers – Gargi, Maitreyi

phases.name: Transition to Mahajanapada Age
points: Entire North India (16 Mahajanapadas)
Decline of Vedic tribal culture; rise of Mahajanapadas
Growth of urbanization, commerce, coinage
New religious movements emerge (Buddhism, Jainism)
Women in early Buddhism & Jainism (Mahaprajapati Gautami and others)

Society: Kinship-based tribal society; families (Kula), clans (Vish), tribes (Jan)
Varna system (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) emerges in Later Vedic period
Varna becomes rigid by the Late Vedic period
Economy: Pastoral economy (cattle = wealth) with limited agriculture in Early Vedic
Agriculture (use of iron plough), surplus production, artisans and crafts in Later Vedic
Monetary economy, long-distance trade and banking develop by the Transition period
Polity: Tribal chiefdoms (Raja, elected); Sabha and Samiti as deliberative assemblies
Janapadas emerge; hereditary kingship stronger; bureaucracy begins
Religion & Philosophy: Nature worship of Devas – Indra, Agni, Varuna, Mitra, Ushas, Soma
Complex Yajnas; rise of Brahmanas (ritual specialists)
Upanishads (major & minor); focus on Brahman, Atman, Karma, Moksha, Rebirth
Rise of Buddhism, Jainism; decline of Vedic ritualism

women.name: Lopamudra
women.note: Composer of hymns in the Rigveda; symbol of intelligence & devotion.

women.name: Apala
women.note: Rigvedic seer; her hymns reflect personal struggles & spiritual quest.

women.name: Ghosha
women.note: Author of hymns in the Rigveda; prayed for health & well-being.

women.name: Vishvavara
women.note: Composer of hymns; participated in philosophical debates.

women.name: Gargi Vachaknavi
women.note: Philosopher; debated with Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

women.name: Maitreyi
women.note: Philosopher; dialogue with Yajnavalkya on Atman & immortality.

women.name: Mahaprajapati Gautami
women.note: Prominent in early Buddhism; first woman to join the Buddha's Sangha.

events.title: Composition of the Rigveda
events.desc: The oldest Vedic Samhita is composed during the Early Vedic Age in the Sapta-Sindhu region.

events.title: Later Vedic texts composed
events.desc: Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda, Brahmanas and Aranyakas are composed as settlement shifts to the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.

events.title: Major Upanishads composed
events.desc: Philosophical inquiry into Brahman, Atman, Karma and Moksha; Gargi and Maitreyi engage in recorded philosophical debate.

events.title: Rise of the 16 Mahajanapadas
events.desc: Political centralization, urbanization and coinage mark the end of the Vedic phase and the transition to the Mahajanapada Age.

people.name: Yajnavalkya
people.note: Central figure of Upanishadic dialogues with Gargi and Maitreyi.

prelims: Rigveda is the earliest text – composed in Sanskrit
Sequence: Early Vedic → Later Vedic → Late Vedic → Upanishadic → Transition
Key texts by phase (see Quick Revision)
mains: Varna system evolved from functional to hereditary and rigid
Political system evolved from tribal assemblies to centralized kingdoms
Religious thought evolved from nature worship/rituals to philosophical inquiry (Upanishads)
Contribution of women in Vedic literature and philosophy

periods.title: Age of Mahajanapadas
periods.tagline: The transition from the Vedic Age to the Age of Empires
periods.overview: Sixteen Mahajanapadas — both monarchies and republics (Gana-Sanghas) — emerge as territorial states with defined boundaries, driving urbanization, economic growth, and religious ferment (rise of Buddhism, Jainism, and other Shramana traditions), before Magadha rises to hegemony and Chandragupta Maurya founds the Mauryan Empire in 321 BCE.

phases.name: Vedic to Janapada Transition
points: Growth of agriculture, iron technology
Permanent settlements & villages
Emergence of tribes into Janapadas

phases.name: Rise of Mahajanapadas
points: 16 Mahajanapadas with defined boundaries
Territorial states with urban centres & trade routes

phases.name: Age of Expansion & Rivalries
points: Expansion of kingdoms; wars and alliances common
Magadha emerges as a dominant power

phases.name: Religious & Intellectual Ferment
points: Rise of Buddhism, Jainism, Ajivikas
Kautilya's Arthashastra; debates on society, dharma, moksha

phases.name: Rise of Magadha
points: Conquest of Anga, Vatsa, Avanti, etc.
Nanda Dynasty rules Magadha

phases.name: Towards Empire
points: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas
Foundation of the Mauryan Empire

Political Development: 16 Mahajanapadas – (i) Monarchies e.g. Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti, Kashi, Anga; (ii) Republics (Gana-Sanghas) e.g. Vajji (Licchavis), Malla, Shakya, Kollya, Bulis
Territorial states with well-defined boundaries and capitals; inter-state rivalries, conquests and alliances common
Magadha emerged as the most powerful state
Administration: Council of Ministers (Mantriparishad) assisted the king; officials like Senapati, Bhandagarika, Dvarpala, Gramika
Republics had assemblies (Sabha, Samiti, Gana); early bureaucracy & record-keeping
Economy: Agriculture the main occupation; iron tools increased productivity
Trade and commerce flourished; use of punch-marked coins (Karshapana)
Urban centres developed: Rajagriha, Vaishali, Ujjain, Kashi, Kaushambi
Society: Varna system existed but more fluid; joint family system prevalent
Artisans, traders (Shreshthis), merchants gained importance; position of women better than in later periods
Slavery existed but not dominant; rise of new social classes
Religion & Philosophy: Rise of Shramana traditions – Buddhism, Jainism, Ajivikas
People dissatisfied with ritualism and social inequalities of Brahmanical traditions
Art, Literature & Culture: Language: Pali, Ardhamagadhi, Prakrits; Sanskrit continued
Buddhist Suttas & Vinaya Pitaka; Jain Agamas; epics continued (Ramayana, Mahabharata compositions)
Military: Large standing armies (in Magadha); elephants, chariots, cavalry, infantry

women.name: Ambapali
women.note: Courtesan of Vaishali; associated with the Buddhist Sangha.

women.name: Gargi & Maitreyi
women.note: Named as examples of women's participation in educational and philosophical debates in this period.

events.title: 16 Mahajanapadas take shape
events.desc: Territorial states with defined boundaries, capitals, administration and standing armies replace tribal janapadas.

events.title: Life of Gautama Buddha
events.desc: Founding of Buddhism amid widespread dissatisfaction with Brahmanical ritualism and social inequality.

events.title: Life of Mahavira
events.desc: Mahavira's teachings establish Jainism as a major Shramana tradition of the period.

events.title: Rise of Magadha and the Nanda Dynasty
events.desc: Magadha conquers Anga, Vatsa, Avanti and other states; the Nanda Dynasty rules before being overthrown.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas
events.desc: Foundation of the Mauryan Empire, ending the Mahajanapada period and beginning the Age of Empires.

prelims: 16 Mahajanapadas – concept, types (monarchy/republic) and list
Role of Buddhism & Jainism in the period
mains: Rise of Magadha – reasons and conquests
Political, economic, social and religious developments of the age
Women's status and contributions in this period

quickFacts: Rise of Magadha & Foundation of the Mauryan Empire

periods.title: The Mauryan Empire
periods.tagline: One of the greatest empires of Ancient India
periods.overview: The Mauryan Empire was the first to politically unify most of India. Founded by Chandragupta Maurya with Chanakya's (Kautilya) help after overthrowing the Nandas, it expanded under Bindusara, reached its golden age of Dhamma and welfare under Ashoka, and declined under weak later rulers before ending around 185 BCE.

phases.name: Rise of the Empire (Pre-Mauryan Background)
points: Nanda Dynasty in Magadha (Mahapadma Nanda)
Chanakya (Kautilya) devises strategy to overthrow the Nandas
Chandragupta Maurya rises with the support of people and allies

phases.name: Chandragupta Maurya
points: Overthrows the Nandas with Chanakya's help; establishes the Mauryan Empire
Defeats Seleucus I Nicator (305 BCE); treaty & marriage alliance; gains western territories (Afghanistan, etc.)
Strong central administration; Megasthenes visits his court

phases.name: Bindusara
points: Son of Chandragupta; extends the empire in the south (Deccan and beyond)
Greek sources call him 'Amitrochates'
Empire expansion continues; strong administration maintained

phases.name: Ashoka the Great
points: Initially Governor of Ujjain; becomes king after a struggle
Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) – turning point of his reign; adopts Dhamma
Extensive edicts and inscriptions; promotes peace, welfare & morality
Greatest Mauryan ruler; spread of Buddhism

phases.name: Later Mauryan Rulers
points: Dasharatha, Samprati and other weak rulers
Provincial governors gain power; central authority weakens; decentralization begins
Empire gradually weakens

phases.name: Decline of Empire
points: Rise of Pushyamitra Shunga (c. 185 BCE)
Last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha Maurya assassinated
End of Mauryan rule; transition to the Shunga dynasty

Political Administration: Centralized monarchy; Council of Ministers (Mantriparishad); Amatyas (officials); provincial & district administration
Under Ashoka: highly centralized rule, Dhamma Mahamatras appointed, regular tours & inspections, record keeping
Decline: central authority weakens, provincial governors powerful, decentralization begins under later rulers
Revenue System: Land revenue (1/4th of produce); taxes on trade, forest, mines, salt; state monopolies on key goods
Under Ashoka: fair taxation, remission in times of flood/drought, welfare orientation
Decline: revenue officials corrupt, burden of taxation increased
Judicial System: King as the highest judge; courts at different levels; Dharma, Vyavahara, Charita as sources
Under Ashoka: emphasis on justice & mercy, death penalty rare, appeals allowed
Military System: Large standing army (6 lakh infantry, 30k cavalry, 9k elephants, 8k chariots – per Greek accounts); well organized
Reduced emphasis on conquest after the Kalinga War; army maintained for protection
Decline: army weakens, frontier provinces lost
Economic Life: Agriculture as mainstay; state control over mines, forests; trade both internal & external; use of punch-marked coins
Promotion of trade, roads, rest houses, wells and protection to merchants under Ashoka
Society: Varna system present but flexible; people loyal to the state; urbanization increased; growth of middle class (merchants, artisans)
Religion: Tolerant towards all religions; Ashoka patronizes Buddhism, respects all sects, promotes Dhamma policy (moral values, not a particular sect)
Art & Architecture: Beginning of grand stone architecture; Pillars, Stupas, Rock-cut edicts; Sarnath Lion Capital; Barabar Caves
Foreign Relations: Treaty with Seleucus I Nicator; Greek ambassador Megasthenes at Chandragupta's court
Ashoka: friendly relations with Hellenistic rulers; missions to Sri Lanka & Central Asia

women.name: Dharma Mahamatra women officials
women.note: Ashoka appointed women Dharma Mahamatras to look after the welfare of women and propagate Dhamma.

women.name: Bhikkhuni Sangha
women.note: Many women joined the Buddhist order during Ashoka's time and contributed to the spread of Buddhism.

women.name: Ashoka's Queens (Queen Devi & Tishyarakshita)
women.note: Mentioned in Buddhist traditions.

women.name: Women in the economy
women.note: Involved in handicrafts, weaving, agriculture, and as owners of property to some extent.

events.title: Foundation of the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nanda dynasty with the strategy and support of Chanakya (Kautilya).

events.title: War with Seleucus I Nicator
events.desc: Chandragupta defeats Seleucus; a treaty and marriage alliance follow, and the Mauryas gain western territories including parts of Afghanistan.

events.title: The Kalinga War
events.desc: Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga, whose bloodshed leads him to adopt Dhamma — a turning point in Mauryan and Indian history.

events.title: Spread of Buddhism under Ashoka
events.desc: Ashoka's edicts, missions, and patronage lead to the wide spread of Buddhism within and beyond India.

events.title: End of the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Pushyamitra Shunga assassinates the last Mauryan ruler, Brihadratha Maurya, ending the dynasty.

people.name: Chandragupta Maurya
people.note: r. c. 322–298 BCE; guided by Chanakya (Kautilya).

people.name: Chanakya (Kautilya)
people.note: Chief architect of Mauryan rise and administration.

people.name: Bindusara
people.note: r. c. 298–273 BCE; called 'Amitrochates' by Greek sources.

people.name: Ashoka the Great
people.note: r. c. 273–232 BCE; adopted Dhamma after the Kalinga War.

people.name: Megasthenes
people.note: Sent by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta's court; author of Indica.

prelims: Founder: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 322 BCE); Greatest ruler: Ashoka the Great
Capital: Pataliputra; Script: Brahmi & Kharoshthi; Official language: Prakrit
Kalinga War, Dhamma, and Ashokan edicts
mains: The Mauryan Empire was the first step towards the political unity of India
Arthashastra as the best source for administration & economy
Ashoka's Dhamma as a welfare-state and social-harmony policy

periods.title: Ashoka the Great
periods.tagline: “Devanampiya Piyadasi” — Beloved of the Gods, He Who Looks with Affection on His Subjects
periods.overview: A dedicated deep-dive on the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, tracing his life from birth and training, through his accession, the transformative Kalinga War, his conversion to Dhamma, and his final years of moral governance and the spread of Buddhism — read alongside the broader Mauryan Empire period.

phases.name: Early Life & Ascent
points: Born to Bindusara and Subhadrangi (traditionally); prince of the Mauryan Empire
Trained in statecraft, warfare and administration; appointed Governor of Ujjain and later Taxila
Became crown prince after Bindusara's reign

phases.name: Coronation as Emperor
points: Ascended the throne in 268 BCE after Bindusara's death
Initially focused on consolidating the vast empire; faced revolts in Taxila, Ujjain and border regions
Efficient administrative reorganisation

phases.name: The Kalinga War
points: Invaded Kalinga (modern Odisha) — one of the bloodiest wars in history with huge loss of life
100,000 killed, 150,000 deported, many more affected (as per Rock Edict XIII)
Deeply moved by the suffering of the people

phases.name: Conversion to Dhamma
points: Renounced violence and adopted 'Dhamma' (righteousness); dedicated his life to the welfare of all beings
Became a patron of Buddhism; promoted peace, tolerance, compassion and moral living

phases.name: Later Years & Death
points: Devoted to spreading Dhamma and welfare activities; regular tours (Dhamma Yatras) to meet people and know their problems
Passed away in 232 BCE at the age of about 56

Political Administration: Before Kalinga: consolidated Mauryan Empire, strong centralised administration, appointed able officials, provincial administration in place
After transformation: continued strong administration, regular tours (Dhamma Yatras), appointed Dhamma-Mahamatras (officers of Dhamma)
Dhamma Policy: Rule based on Dhamma, not conquest; welfare measures for all sections; hospitals for humans and animals
Rest houses, wells, shade trees; cleanliness and public health; standard weights & measures, control over prices of commodities
Religion: Patron of all religions; personally inclined towards Buddhism even before Kalinga; became a devoted Buddhist and promoted Buddha's teachings
Built stupas and monuments; supported the Sangha (Buddhist order); allowed freedom of religion; did not impose Buddhism on others
Achievements & Impact: Stable and prosperous empire; encouraged just trade and fairness; welfare of farmers, traders, workers
Kindness, humility, truthfulness; respect for all sects; brotherhood and harmony; victory through Dhamma (moral victory) over military victory
Spread of Buddhism in India and abroad; religious tolerance set an example

women.name: Queen Tissarakkha
women.note: One of Ashoka's wives, mentioned in Buddhist tradition.

women.name: Sanghamitra
women.note: Daughter of Ashoka and Queen Devi, sent to Sri Lanka to spread Buddhism; took the sacred Bodhi tree (from Bodh Gaya) to Sri Lanka.

women.name: Women in Society under Ashoka
women.note: Ashoka's Dhamma promoted respect for women, equality and moral values; his inscriptions show concern for women's welfare and protection.

events.title: Ashoka's accession
events.desc: Ashoka ascends the Mauryan throne after Bindusara's death and begins consolidating the vast empire.

events.title: The Kalinga War
events.desc: The invasion of Kalinga causes immense loss of life and deeply moves Ashoka, becoming the turning point of his reign.

events.title: Ashoka adopts Dhamma
events.desc: Ashoka renounces violence, embraces Dhamma (righteousness), and dedicates his rule to the welfare of all beings.

events.title: Dhamma missions sent abroad
events.desc: Missions are sent to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitta), Gandhara, Kashmir-Himalayas, Suvarnabhumi (SE Asia), and Hellenistic kingdoms to the west.

events.title: Death of Ashoka
events.desc: Ashoka dies at about age 56, leaving behind a model of ethical governance and inscriptions that remain a valuable historical source.

people.name: Ashoka the Great
people.note: r. 268–232 BCE; known as Devanampiya Piyadasi; the greatest Mauryan ruler.

people.name: Bindusara
people.note: Second Mauryan emperor.

prelims: First ruler to adopt Dhamma as the basis of governance
Known as Devanampiya Piyadasi; capital Pataliputra; turned to Buddhism after the Kalinga War (261 BCE)
Sources: 14 Major Rock Edicts, 7 Pillar Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Cave Inscriptions, Greek Accounts (Megasthenes)
mains: Ashoka the Great is the best example of Dhamma-based governance
The Kalinga War was the turning point in his life; his edicts are important for understanding ancient India
He promoted welfare, tolerance and peace; the spread of Buddhism in India and abroad was his greatest legacy

periods.title: Post Mauryan Period
periods.tagline: Fragmentation of the Mauryan Empire • Rise of Regional Powers • Cultural & Economic Flourishing • Religious Pluralism
periods.overview: Following the fragmentation of the Mauryan Empire, a mosaic of regional and foreign-origin dynasties — Shungas, Kanvas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Sindhu-Sakas (Western Satraps), early Pallavas, and the Kushan Empire — rule simultaneously, producing extensive trade (including with Rome), cultural synthesis, and religious pluralism, and laying the foundation for the Gupta Age.

phases.name: Shunga Empire
points: Pushyamitra Shunga overthrows the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha
Capital Pataliputra (later Vidisha); Ashvamedha sacrifices performed
Patronage to Brahmanical religion; declines with rise of the Kanvas

phases.name: Kanva Dynasty
points: Founded by Vasudeva (a minister) who overthrows the Shungas
Capital at Pataliputra; weak rulers, power in hands of ministers & generals
Ended by rise of regional powers

phases.name: Satavahanas
points: Large empire in the Deccan & parts of North India; capital Pratishthana (Paithan)
Strong under Gautamiputra Satakarni; first great power of the Deccan connecting north-south trade

phases.name: Indo-Greeks
points: Greek rulers after the Bactrian Greeks in NW India
Menander (Milinda) most famous; patron of Buddhism; bilingual (Greek & Kharoshthi) coins

phases.name: Sindhu-Saka (Western Satraps)
points: Sakas from Central Asia; capital at Ujjain
Rudradaman I (greater ruler); control over Malwa, Gujarat, Kathiawar; Junagadh inscription (Sanskrit)

phases.name: Pallavas (Early)
points: Early Pallavas emerge in the Tamil region; capital Kanchipuram
Simhavishnu expands power; promoted Brahmanism, art & culture; foundation of later Pallava power

phases.name: Kushan Empire (Late Phase)
points: Kanishka (most notable), Huvishka, Vasudeva
Buddhism flourishes (especially Mahayana); Gandhara art develops
Trade with Rome, China; decline in the 3rd century

Political: Political decentralization but cultural unity across many regional powers
Economy: Trade & urban centres thrive; prosperous trade ports; Indo-Roman trade (gold inflow)
Coinage in silver & copper across most dynasties
Society: Cultural fusion; guilds (Shrenis) active; women had some freedom in parts of this period
Social stratification continued under most dynasties
Religion: Coexistence of Buddhism, Jainism, Brahmanism; Kanishka patronized Buddhism (4th Buddhist Council under his tradition)
Revival of Brahmanism; rise of Puranic religion
Art & Culture: Bharhut, Sanchi railings; Yakshi sculptures, pillars
Gandhara art (Greek influence); Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda art

women.name: Gautami Balashri (Satavahana Queen)
women.note: Mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni; her Nasik inscription praises her piety & charity.

women.name: Naganika (Satavahana Queen)
women.note: Performed Hiranyagarbha & other Vedic rituals; Naneghat inscription.

events.title: Kanishka and the height of the Kushan Empire

events.title: Rudradaman I and the Junagadh inscription
events.desc: The Western Satrap ruler Rudradaman I issues the Junagadh rock inscription, an early major Sanskrit inscription.

people.note: Overthrew Brihadratha Maurya c. 185 BCE.

people.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni
people.note: Made the Satavahanas the first great Deccan power.

people.name: Menander (Milinda)

Indo-Greeks & Sakas contributed to cultural synthesis

Trade with Rome brought prosperity; growth of art, architecture and literature

Trade, cultural synthesis, religious tolerance, art & literature growth

periods.title: The Gupta Age
periods.tagline: The Golden Age of India
periods.overview: Called the 'Golden Age of India', the Gupta Age is marked by political unity and stability under strong rulers, well-organized administration, agricultural and trade-driven economic prosperity, flourishing art/literature/science, and religious tolerance — before Huna invasions and feudalism led to decline.

phases.name: Chandragupta I
points: Founded the Gupta Empire; married Kumaradevi (Lichchhavi princess), strengthening Gupta power through alliance
Received the title 'Maharajadhiraja'; control over Magadha; consolidation of power

phases.name: Samudragupta
points: Great conqueror & empire builder; conquests across Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha
Policy of 'Conquest, but not annexation' for southern kings
Allahabad Pillar Inscription (composed by Harishena); received the title 'Prayagpriya'

phases.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
points: Defeated the Shakas (Western Kshatrapas); conquest of Malwa, Gujarat, Saurashtra
Ujjain became the second capital; patron of art, literature, culture; Navaratna (Nine Gems) in his court
Greatest ruler of the Gupta age; title 'Vikramaditya' after Shakari victory

phases.name: Kumaragupta I
points: Empire extended & stable; revolt of Pushyamitras suppressed
Patron of learning & religion; many land grants issued

phases.name: Skandagupta
points: Faced and successfully resisted Huna invasions; restored the empire's glory
Repaired the Sudarshan Lake (Junagadh); last great ruler of the Gupta Empire

phases.name: Later Guptas
points: Weak rulers; feudatories gain power; Huna invasions intensify
Political disintegration; end of Gupta political unity; rise of regional kingdoms

Political Administration: Hereditary monarchy; centralized administration; efficient bureaucracy; empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces)
Economy: Agriculture main occupation; land revenue important; flourishing trade (internal & external); use of gold coins (Dinar)
Society: Based on the Varna system; joint family system; status of women improved in some respects; growth of towns
Religion: Hinduism dominant (Vaishnavism); Buddhism & Jainism also flourished; religious tolerance; temple building advanced
Art & Architecture: Classical age of Indian art; development of sculpture, painting, temple architecture; Udayagiri caves, Deogarh temple; Ajanta paintings (early phase)
Literature: Sanskrit literature at its peak (classical period); Kalidasa, Aryabhata (mathematics, astronomy), Varahamihira, Vishakhadatta, Shudraka
Science & Technology: Advancement in astronomy, mathematics, medicine (invention of zero concept); development of the Aryabhatiya
Foreign Relations: Relations with China, SE Asia; diplomatic & trade contacts; Chinese pilgrim Faxian visited India

women.name: Kumaradevi (Lichchhavi Princess)
women.note: Marriage with Chandragupta I strengthened Gupta power through the Lichchhavi alliance.

women.name: Prabhavati Gupta
women.note: Daughter of Chandragupta II; Queen of the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. Acted as regent and issued land grants.

women.name: Anantadevi
women.note: Queen of Kumaragupta I; known from inscriptions; made religious donations & grants.

women.name: Achana Devi
women.note: Wife of Skandagupta; mentioned in inscriptions; noted political role during times of crisis.

women.name: Women's Status in the Gupta Age
women.note: Women could own property (Stridhan); enjoyed rights in education & religion; participation in arts, literature & family life; noted women queens & regents existed.

events.title: Foundation of the Gupta Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire and consolidates power in Magadha, strengthened by the Lichchhavi marriage alliance.

events.title: Samudragupta's conquests
events.desc: Extensive military campaigns across Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha, recorded on the Allahabad Pillar Inscription.

events.title: Chandragupta II defeats the Shakas
events.desc: Conquest of Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra; the Gupta Age reaches its cultural and territorial peak.

events.title: Skandagupta repels the Hunas
events.desc: Successful resistance against Huna invasions preserves the empire, though at growing cost.

events.title: End of Gupta political unity
events.desc: Weak later rulers, resurgent feudatories and renewed Huna pressure bring about the disintegration of the Gupta Empire.

people.name: Samudragupta
people.note: r. c. 335–375 CE; great conqueror & empire builder.

people.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
people.note: r. c. 375–415 CE; greatest ruler of the Gupta age.

people.name: Kalidasa

people.name: Aryabhata

people.name: Faxian

prelims: The Gupta Age is called the 'Golden Age of India'
Political unity and stability under strong rulers
Development of art, literature, science & education
mains: Samudragupta's conquests and Chandragupta II's victories over the Shakas
Well-organized administration & efficient revenue system
Religious tolerance and flourishing of Hinduism, Buddhism & Jainism
Decline due to weak successors, invasions (Hunas), feudalism & economic decline

periods.title: Post Gupta Age
periods.tagline: Age of Regional Kingdoms • Political Fragmentation but Cultural Flowering • Rise of New Powers • Growth of Bhakti
periods.overview: After Gupta unity ends, a set of regional kingdoms — Maitrakas, Pushyabhutis/Vardhanas (including Harsha), Chalukyas of Badami, Pallavas, Gauras-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, and Palas — rule concurrently, transitioning India from the ancient to the medieval period through political fragmentation, continuing cultural unity, and the foundation for the tripartite struggle among the Rashtrakutas, Palas and Pratiharas.

phases.name: Maitrakas
points: Rule in Gujarat (Valabhi); important power in Western India; sea trade & temple construction
Udayasena constitutes Valabhi University; patronage to Buddhism and Jainism

phases.name: Pushyabhutis / Vardhanas
points: Capital at Sthanesvara (Thanesar); notable rulers Prabhakaravardhana, Harshavardhana
Harsha becomes emperor (c. 606 CE); conquests in North India; Chinese traveller Xuanzang visits India (c. 629–645 CE)

phases.name: Chalukyas (Badami)
points: Founded by Pulakeshin I; great ruler Pulakeshin II (Vatapi); capital Vatapi (Badami)
Victorious over Kadambas, Alupas, Mauryas; fought Chalukya-Pallava wars with Pallava king Mahendravarman I

phases.name: Pallavas (Continued)
points: Capital Kanchipuram; notable rulers Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla)
Defeated Chalukya Pulakeshin II (Nagabhata I); great patrons of art & architecture (Shore Temple, Mamallapuram)

phases.name: Gauras – Pratiharas
points: Gurjara-Pratiharas emerge in Rajasthan; Nagabhata I resists Arab invaders
Arab expansion checked in western India; rise as a major power in North India

phases.name: Rashtrakutas
points: Emerged from the Deccan (Manyakheta); founder Dantidurga
Overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami (753 CE); strong empire under Krishna I

phases.name: Palas
points: Emerged in Bengal & Bihar; founder Gopala (elected by feudatories)
Strong rulers Dharmapala, Devapala; patrons of Mahayana Buddhism; Nalanda University flourished

Political: Political decentralization (decline of Gupta power leads to rise of regional kingdoms & dynasties)
Religion: Growth of the Bhakti movement gains strength; temples, art & architecture witness regional styles
Buddhism flourished in East (Palas), Jainism in West & Deccan; Ellora caves symbolize tolerance
Economy: Land grants, temple economy; growth of trade, urban decline in some regions
Society: Caste system continued; joint family system continued; women had limited rights but queens active in administration & grants in some kingdoms; education through Gurukuls & Universities (Nalanda, Valabhi)

women.name: Rudramadevi (Early Chalukya)
women.note: Known for bravery & administration.

women.name: Leelavati (Mathematician)
women.note: Her work in mathematics is still remembered.

women.name: Andal (Alvar Saint)
women.note: Composed Tiruppavai in Tamil.

women.name: Akkamahadevi (Veerashaiva Saint)
women.note: Poet-saint from Karnataka.

women.name: Prabhavati Gupta
women.note: Records in copper plates, patron of religion.

events.title: Harshavardhana becomes emperor
events.desc: Harsha rises to power from Thanesar and unites much of North India; author of the play Ratnavali.

events.title: Xuanzang visits India
events.desc: The Chinese traveller Xuanzang's account provides a key source for Harsha's reign and contemporary Indian society.

events.title: Battle of Vatapi
events.desc: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) defeats the Chalukya ruler Pulakeshin II.

events.title: Rashtrakutas overthrow the Chalukyas of Badami
events.desc: Dantidurga establishes Rashtrakuta power in the Deccan, laying groundwork for the later tripartite struggle.

people.name: Harshavardhana

people.name: Pulakeshin II
people.note: Great Chalukya ruler; fought the Pallavas.

periods.title: Early Medieval Period
periods.tagline: Rise of Regional Kingdoms • Political Fragmentation • Cultural & Religious Flourishing • Bhakti Movement • Foundation of Medieval India
periods.overview: The Early Medieval Period is dominated by the tripartite struggle for control of Kannauj among the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas, alongside powerful regional dynasties in the North (Chalukyas of Kalyani, Paramaras, Chandelas, Senas) and South (Cholas, Chalukyas, Pandyas, Cheras, Hoysalas, Yadavas). It closes with Turkish invasions and the transition to the Delhi Sultanate.

phases.name: Early Rajput Period
points: Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Palas emerge
Arab invasions in Sindh (711 CE) – limited success; rise of Rajput clans

phases.name: Pratihara Empire
points: Capital Kannauj; powerful ruler Mihir Bhoja
Defended against Arabs; tripartite struggle with Palas & Rashtrakutas

phases.name: Rashtrakuta Empire
points: Capital Manyakheta; great rulers Dantidurga, Krishna I, Govinda III, Amoghavarsha I
Patrons of art, literature & Jainism

phases.name: Pala Empire
points: Capital Pataliputra, later Vikramashila; great rulers Gopala, Dharmapala, Devapala
Buddhist universities Nalanda revived; Pala-Sena style of art

phases.name: Chola Empire
points: Capital Thanjavur; great rulers Vijayalaya, Aditya I, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I
Maritime power; temple economy; administration model; overseas trade

phases.name: Chalukyas of Kalyani
points: Capital Kalyani; great ruler Vikramaditya VI
Conflict with Cholas; promoted art, literature (Kannada)

phases.name: Paramaras, Chandelas, Senas & Others
points: Paramaras (Malwa): Bhoja; Chandelas (Bundelkhand): Khajuraho temples
Senas (Bengal): Ballala Sena; Gahadavalas (Kannauj): Jayachandra

phases.name: Turkish Invasions & Transition
points: Mahmud of Ghazni (1000–1027 CE) – multiple invasions; Muhammad Ghori (late 12th c.) laid foundation of the Delhi Sultanate
End of the early medieval period; beginning of a new phase

Political Administration: Feudal polity common; kingship generally hereditary; samantas/feudatories important across most kingdoms
Economy: Agriculture main occupation, land revenue main source; trade through land & rivers (North); overseas trade with SE Asia & China (South, e.g. Cholas)
Society: Caste system more rigid; rise of Rajput clans in the North; village communities and local self-government strong in the South (Sabhas, Ur, Nagaram)
Religion: Patronage to Hinduism (Vaishnavism & Shaivism); Jainism also supported (esp. West/Deccan); Bhakti Movement grew (Alvars, Nayanars, Basavanna, Ramanuja, Madhva etc.)
Art & Architecture: Nagara style temples in the North (Khajuraho, Osian, Gwalior); Dravidian style architecture peaks in the South (Brihadeeswara Temple, Chola bronzes – Nataraja)
Literature: Sanskrit literature patronized widely; regional literatures develop – Kannada (Kavirajamarga), Tamil (Tevaram, Divya Prabandham), Bengali (Charyapada)

events.desc: Early Arab incursions into Sindh meet limited success against the wider subcontinent.

events.title: Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj
events.desc: The Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas contest control of Kannauj for political supremacy in North India.

events.title: Rajaraja Chola I's reign
events.desc: The Chola Empire becomes a major maritime and temple-building power under Rajaraja I and his successor Rajendra I.

events.title: Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions
events.desc: Repeated raids into North India weaken regional kingdoms and foreshadow later Turkish conquest.

events.title: Muhammad Ghori's campaigns
events.desc: Ghori's conquests lay the foundation for the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate.

people.name: Mihir Bhoja
people.note: One of the most powerful Pratihara emperors.

people.name: Rajaraja Chola I
people.note: Built the Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur; expanded Chola maritime power.

people.note: Patron of art, literature and Jainism.

periods.title: Kingdoms of the North
periods.tagline: Rise of Regional Power • Political Fragmentation • Cultural & Religious Flourishing • Temple Architecture
periods.overview: A detailed regional study of the northern kingdoms of the Early Medieval Period: the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, Rashtrakuta influence in the North, Kalachuris (Tripuri), Chahamanas (Chauhans), Paramaras, Chandelas, and the Gurjara Solankis (Chalukyas) of Anhilwara — each with distinctive administration, economy, religion and art, culminating in the Ghaznavid and Ghurid invasions that opened the way to the Delhi Sultanate.

phases.name: Pratihara Empire
points: Gurjara-Pratiharas emerged as the most powerful in North India; capital Kannauj (changed)
Strong rulers Nagabhata I, Mihir Bhoja, Mahendrapala I; repelled Arab invasions in Sindh

phases.name: Pala Empire
points: Rulers of Bengal & Bihar; founder Gopala (elected by nobles)
Greatest rulers Dharmapala, Devapala; patron of Buddhism, Nalanda University; extended influence in North India

phases.name: Rashtrakuta Influence in North
points: Though Deccan based, influenced North India; rulers Dantidurga, Krishna I, Govinda III
Defeated Pratiharas & Palas at times; patron of art, literature & Jainism

phases.name: Kalachuris (Tripuri)
points: Ruled Central India (Tripuri); rulers Kokalla I, Yuvarajadeva I
Conflict with Paramaras & Chandelas; Shaivism predominant

phases.name: Chahamanas (Chauhans)
points: Capital Shakambhari (Sambhar), later Ajmer; important rulers Vigraharaja IV, Prithviraj III
Defeated Ghazni once (Tarain I, 1191); patron of Sanskrit literature & temples

phases.name: Paramaras
points: Capital Ujjain, later Dhar; ruler Bhoja (greatest, scholar-writer of the Samarangana Sutradhara)
Patron of art, architecture, learning

phases.name: Chandelas
points: Capital Khajuraho, Mahoba; rulers Yashovarman, Dhanga, Vidyadhara
Built magnificent temples at Khajuraho; repelled Ghaznavid attacks

phases.name: Gurjara Solankis (Chalukyas) of Anhilwara
points: Capital Anhilwara (Patan); rulers Mularaja, Bhima I, Siddharaja Jayasimha
Patron of Jainism, art, architecture; advanced administration & irrigation

events.title: Second Battle of Tarain

Pratiharas, Palas, Chahamanas, Paramaras, Chandelas, Solankis, Kalachuris

periods.title: Kingdoms of the South
periods.tagline: Rise of Powerful South Indian Kingdoms • Consolidation & Temple Culture • Maritime Power
periods.overview: While the North fragments politically, South India sees stronger consolidation under the Pallavas, the great Chola Empire, the Pandya Kingdom, the Cheras, the Western Chalukyas, the Hoysalas, and the Yadavas of Devagiri — marked by temple architecture, maritime trade, and vibrant regional literatures, before internal conflicts open the door to the Delhi Sultanate's southward expansion (Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Devagiri in 1296).

phases.name: Pallava Empire
points: Capital Kanchipuram; great rulers Nandivarman II, Dantivarman
Defeated by the Cholas in the late 9th century; patrons of Shaivism & Vaishnavism

phases.name: Chola Empire
points: Capital Thanjavur, later Gangaikonda Cholapuram; great rulers Vijayalaya, Aditya I, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I, Kulottunga I
Built a vast empire & strong navy; Golden Age of Chola power & culture

phases.name: Pandya Kingdom
points: Capital Madurai; great rulers Maravarman Rajasimha, Jatavarman Sundara Pandya
Famous for pearl trade & Tamil culture; rivalry with the Cholas for dominance

phases.name: Cheras (Kerala)
points: Region: Kerala & western coast; capital Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur)
Rulers Kulasekhara, Rama Varma; strong maritime trade with Arabs, China; patronized temples, education & trade

phases.name: Western Chalukyas
points: Capital Kalyani; great rulers Tailapa II, Vikramaditya VI, Someshwara I
Conflict with the Cholas for Vengi & Karnataka; famous for architecture at Pattadakal, Aihole

phases.name: Hoysalas
points: Capital Belur, Halebidu; great rulers Vishnuvardhana, Ballala II
Built exquisite temples: Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura; supported Jainism alongside Hinduism

phases.name: Yadavas of Devagiri
points: Capital Devagiri (Daulatabad); important rulers Bhillama V, Jaitugi
Controlled parts of Maharashtra & Karnataka; later defeated by Alauddin Khalji (1296 CE)

events.title: Rajaraja Chola I builds the Brihadeeswara Temple

events.title: Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Devagiri

people.name: Rajaraja Chola I

people.name: Rajendra Chola I

periods.title: The Delhi Sultanate
periods.tagline: Establishment of Turkish Rule in India • Political Consolidation & Expansion • Administrative & Economic Developments • Cultural Synthesis
periods.overview: The Delhi Sultanate spans five dynasties over 320 years — Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi — establishing the first Islamic kingdom in India, introducing new administrative systems (the Iqta system), spreading Islam and Sufism, developing Indo-Islamic architecture, and ultimately laying the foundation for the Mughal Empire after Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi in 1526.

phases.name: Mamluk / Slave Dynasty
points: Key rulers: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia Sultan, Balban
Laid the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate; consolidated Turkish rule in North India; central administration
Built the Qutub Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque

phases.name: Khalji Dynasty
points: Key rulers: Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah
Expansion of the empire to South India; strong centralisation & reforms
Alauddin Khalji's military campaigns & conquests; built Siri Fort, Alai Darwaza

phases.name: Tughlaq Dynasty
points: Key rulers: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firuz Shah Tughlaq
Administrative & territorial expansion; token currency and Doab tax experiments under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Firuz Shah's irrigation & public works; built Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad

phases.name: Sayyid Dynasty
points: Key rulers: Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, Alauddin Alam Shah
Considered puppet rulers under Timurid influence; limited control over territories; lost provinces to regional kingdoms

phases.name: Lodi Dynasty
points: Key rulers: Bahlul Lodi, Sikandar Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi
Afghan rule with emphasis on nobility; Sikandar Lodi's administrative reforms strengthened agriculture & trade
Defeated by Babur in 1526 (First Battle of Panipat) – end of the Sultanate

Political Administration: Mamluk: strong monarchy but limited resources; Iqta system introduced; central departments under Diwan-i-Wizarat
Khalji: strong centralisation under Alauddin; Department of Wizarat, Ariz, Barid, etc.; spy system (Barid-i-Mamalik); strict control over nobles
Tughlaq: highly centralised but frequent revolts; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious but mostly failed experiments; Firoz Shah emphasises decentralisation
Sayyid: weak central authority; nobles gain power; many territories become independent
Lodi: Afghan nobility influential; Sikandar Lodi's reorganisation; princely provinces under governors
Economy: Agriculture mainstay; Iqta system for revenue collection; development of cities & trade
Khalji: land revenue reforms, market control & price regulation, state monopolies on horses/liquor etc., promotion of trade & commerce
Tughlaq: Doab tax & token currency (Muhammad bin Tughlaq); irrigation works (Firoz Shah); trade through ports & inland
Lodi: agriculture improved; Sikandar Lodi's canals & gardens; growth of trade, especially in Punjab
Society: Turkish dominance in administration; society divided into Ashraf & Ajlaf; status based on religion & birth
Khalji: more social mobility; rise of new classes (merchants)
Afghan dominance under the Lodis; integration of different communities; growth of peasantry
Religion: Sunni Islam dominant; Sufism spread (Chishti, Suhrawardi); tolerance towards other religions
Islam strengthened; Sufis had great influence; some persecution of Hindus (Alauddin); Jizya imposed on non-Muslims (Firoz Shah)
Architecture: Indo-Islamic style begins – Qutub Minar, Qutb Complex, Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (Mamluk)
Siri Fort, Alai Darwaza, expansion of mosque architecture (Khalji)
Tughlaqabad Fort, Jahanpanah, Firoz Shah Kotla, Hauz Khas, use of sloping walls & rubble masonry (Tughlaq)
Literature & Learning: Persian official language; works of Minhaj-i-Siraj (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri); translation movement begins
Persian literature flourished under the Khaljis; Amir Khusrau – poetry, music; works of Ziauddin Barani, Isami
Scholars like Ibn Battuta visited under the Tughlaqs

Founder: Qutb-ud-din Aibak; End: defeat of Ibrahim Lodi (1526) by Babur
