periods.title: Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty
periods.tagline: Military Aristocracy – Iqta System – Administrative Reforms – Strong Defence against Mongols
periods.overview: The first and longest-ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. Through Iltutmish's consolidation, Razia Sultan's brief and remarkable reign, and Balban's strong centralisation, the Mamluks established the administrative, military and cultural framework that would underpin later Sultanate rule, before declining into factionalism and giving way to the Khaljis.

phases.name: Qutb-ud-din Aibak
points: Founder of the Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty; laid the foundation of Turkish rule in North India
Began the Qutub Minar; laid the foundation of the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque; Iqta system introduced on a larger scale

phases.name: Aram Shah
points: Weak and unpopular ruler; killed by nobles after a short period of instability and aristocratic intrigue

phases.name: Shams-ud-din Iltutmish
points: Real founder of Delhi Sultanate authority; reorganized the Iqta system
Consolidated 'Chahalgani' (Group of Forty Turkish nobles); introduced silver 'Tanka' and copper 'Jital'; obtained recognition from the Caliph of Baghdad

phases.name: Razia Sultan
points: First and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; capable and just administrator
Tried to reduce the power of Turkish nobles; faced opposition due to gender; deposed after a short but remarkable rule

phases.name: Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (under Balban as Naib)
points: Real authority rested with Balban; central authority strengthened; control over nobles increased

phases.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban
points: Absolute monarchy; theory of Kingship 'Zill-e-Ilahi'; strict court etiquette (Sijda, Paibos); efficient spy system (Barid)
Successfully resisted Mongol invasions; strengthened frontier defence

phases.name: Kaikubad & Last Mamluks
points: Weak rulers; influence of nobles increased; disorder and factionalism; rise of slave aristocracy
Overthrown by Jalal-ud-din Khalji (1290 CE)

women.name: Razia Sultan
women.note: r. 1236–1240; first woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; capable, just and progressive.

events.title: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Mamluk Dynasty
events.desc: Consolidation of Turkish rule in North India begins; construction of the Qutub Minar started.

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Sultanate
events.desc: Central authority strengthened; the Iqta system reorganised; the silver Tanka and copper Jital introduced.

events.title: Razia Sultan's reign
events.desc: The first woman ruler of the Sultanate; opposed by Turkish nobles and eventually deposed.

events.title: Balban's centralisation
events.desc: Absolute monarchy strengthened; strict court discipline enforced; successful defence against Mongol invasions.

events.title: Fall of the Mamluk Dynasty
events.desc: The last Mamluk ruler Kaiqubad/Kaikubad is overthrown; Jalal-ud-din Khalji founds the Khalji Dynasty.

people.name: Shams-ud-din Iltutmish
people.note: r. 1211–1236; real founder of the Sultanate's stable authority.

people.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban
people.note: r. 1266–1287; theory of 'Zill-e-Ilahi' (Shadow of God).

prelims: First and longest dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate
Iqta system was the backbone of administration
Silver 'Tanka' coin introduced by Iltutmish
mains: Iltutmish's administration and Balban's reforms strengthened the state
Successful defence against Mongols ensured stability in North India
Growth of Indo-Islamic culture and institutions in this period

periods.title: Khalji Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Period of Expansion, Administrative Reforms, Economic Prosperity and Military Glory
periods.overview: The first Turkic dynasty after the Mamluks, founded by Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji. Under Alauddin Khalji the empire reached its greatest geographical extent along with sweeping administrative, economic and military reforms, before relaxation of these policies under Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Shah and the brief, unstable rule of Khusro Khan brought the dynasty to an end.

phases.name: Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji
points: Founder of the Khalji Dynasty; overthrew the Mamluks in 1290
Adopted a policy of conciliation; strengthened the state and won popularity

phases.name: Alauddin Khalji
points: Great conqueror & administrator; extended the empire from Gujarat to Bengal and from the Himalayas to the Deccan
Market reforms, revenue reforms, military reforms, strict law & order; highly centralised administration with a strong espionage network (Barid, Munhiyan)
Land revenue reforms (measurement & cash payment); price control of essential goods; abolition of intermediaries

phases.name: Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Shah Khalji
points: Soft-natured compared to Alauddin; took interest in pleasures and religion; gave freedom to nobles
Repealed many of Alauddin's strict policies; nobles regained power; leniency led to decline in central authority

phases.name: Khusro Khan
points: Converted to Islam and gained power; murdered Mubarak Shah and usurped the throne
Short and unpopular rule; overthrown by Ghazi Malik (founder of the Tughlaq Dynasty) in 1320

Political Administration: Jalal-ud-din: mild and conciliatory policy, gave importance to justice & welfare
Alauddin: highly centralised administration, strong espionage network, efficient revenue & military system, district administration under Shiqdar & Amil
Mubarak Shah: relaxed control over administration, gave high positions to favourites, nobles became powerful
Khusro Khan: depended on a few supporters, no strong administrative base
Economy: Alauddin's land revenue reforms and market reforms (price control of essential goods); state control over trade, grains & markets
Mubarak Shah repealed many of Alauddin's economic restrictions; prices rose again
Military: Alauddin: large standing army, branding of horses (Dag) & registration of soldiers (Chehra), regular cash payment; defeated the Mongols repeatedly
Mubarak Shah: army discipline declined, corruption increased
Religion: Jalal-ud-din: Sunni Muslim, tolerant towards Hindus
Alauddin: strict Sunni ruler; persecution of certain groups (especially Mongols); supported Islam
Mubarak Shah: more liberal & tolerant; interested in Sufism
Art & Architecture: Alai Darwaza (begun under Jalal-ud-din, completed under Alauddin), Alai Minar (unfinished), Siri Fort, Hauz-i-Alai
Literature & Culture: Persian was the court language under Alauddin; patronage to Amir Khusrau (poet, musician) and other scholars & Sufis

women.name: Malika-i-Jahan
women.note: Played an important role in administration during Alauddin's Deccan campaigns; other royal women influenced court politics through their connections.

events.title: Jalal-ud-din founds the Khalji Dynasty
events.desc: The Khaljis overthrow the Mamluks, ending the Slave Dynasty and beginning the first Turkic dynasty after them.

events.title: Alauddin Khalji's reign and reforms
events.desc: The empire reaches its maximum geographical extent under Alauddin, accompanied by market, revenue, and military reforms.

events.title: Defeat of Mongol invasions
events.desc: Alauddin Khalji repeatedly defeats Mongol incursions, strengthening the northwest frontier.

events.title: End of the Khalji Dynasty
events.desc: Khusro Khan's short, unpopular rule ends when he is overthrown by Ghazi Malik, who founds the Tughlaq Dynasty.

people.name: Alauddin Khalji
people.note: r. 1296–1316; greatest Khalji ruler; empire reached its maximum extent under him.

people.name: Amir Khusrau
people.note: Prominent at Alauddin's court; associated with the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya.

people.name: Ziauddin Barani
people.note: Author of the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, a key primary source for the period.

prelims: First Turkic dynasty after the Mamluks
Under Alauddin Khalji, the empire reached its maximum geographical extent
Alauddin's market reforms are a classic UPSC topic
mains: Alauddin Khalji's reforms are a model of good governance for the period
Economic control & intelligence system were unique features of his rule
Decline due to relaxation of policies and the rise of nobles under Mubarak Shah

periods.title: Tughlaq Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Period of Experimentation, Administrative Reforms, Economic Policies, Military Campaigns and Architectural Grandeur
periods.overview: The Tughlaq Dynasty, the third dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, spans four phases of rule — Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq's founding, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's bold and often disastrous experiments, Firuz Shah Tughlaq's welfare-oriented stabilisation, and the weak Later Tughlaqs — before Timur's invasion of 1398 shattered the empire and hastened its end in 1414.

phases.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq
points: Founder of the Tughlaq Dynasty; re-established strong central authority
Built the Tughlaqabad Fort (1321 CE); controlled Mongol threats
Promoted agriculture and irrigation; strict revenue collection and law & order

phases.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
points: One of the ablest but most controversial rulers of India; extended the empire from Bengal to the Indus and from the Himalayas to the Krishna River
Bold and largely unsuccessful experiments: token currency, capital shift (Delhi to Daulatabad), Doab revenue increase, agricultural reforms, Khalisa land expansion
Promoted learning, scholars & intellectuals despite frequent revolts and discontent

phases.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
points: Strengthened administration; many welfare and public works projects
Reduction in land revenue; abolition of some harsh taxes; promotion of irrigation & canals
Compiled the 'Fatawa-i-Firuz Shahi'; established new towns and cities

phases.name: Later Tughlaqs
points: Weak & ineffective rulers; nobles became powerful; provinces became independent
Timur's invasion (1398 CE) shakes the empire; repeated revolts and invasions
Decline of central authority and disintegration of the Tughlaq Empire

Political Administration: Ghiyas-ud-din: centralised administration, strong monarch & disciplined army, reorganised Iqta system
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: highly centralised but harsh, introduced Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (revenue), stringent control over officials
Firuz Shah: well-organised bureaucracy, departmental administration, emphasis on written records
Later Tughlaqs: weak central authority, provinces acted independently, nobles became hereditary & powerful
Economy: Ghiyas-ud-din: land revenue main source, agriculture encouraged
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Doab revenue increase (harsh), token currency experiment, Khalisa land expansion, trade & commerce encouraged
Firuz Shah: reduced land revenue, abolition of many taxes (jizya on Hindus abolished), encouraged agriculture, trade & crafts
Later Tughlaqs: economic instability, disruption of trade, heavy taxation by nobles
Military: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: large standing army, conquests in South India, Gujarat, Bengal
Firuz Shah: large but defensive army, focus on fortification
Later Tughlaqs: army weakened, unable to resist Timur
Architecture & Public Works: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Jahanpanah City, Adilabad Fort (Daulatabad)
Firuz Shah: many cities – Firozabad, Firozpur, canals, gardens, madrasas, hospitals, Ashokan pillars installed
Later Tughlaqs: little construction, many earlier works neglected
Religion: Ghiyas-ud-din: Sunni Muslim, tolerant towards non-Muslims
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Sunni Muslim, debated scholars of all religions
Firuz Shah: Sunni orthodox, patron of ulama, some conservative policies
Later Tughlaqs: intolerance increased, religious persecution in some areas

women.name: Taj-ud-din Firuz Shah's queen(s)
women.note: Supported charitable works during Firuz Shah's reign; women from royal families took interest in religious & public works.

events.title: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq founds the dynasty
events.desc: Re-establishes strong central authority in the Delhi Sultanate after the Khaljis; builds the Tughlaqabad Fort.

events.title: Capital shift to Daulatabad
events.desc: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's controversial transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, one of several bold administrative experiments.

events.title: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's welfare reign
events.desc: Abolition of harsh taxes, major irrigation and public works, and the compilation of the Fatawa-i-Firuz Shahi.

events.title: Timur's invasion of Delhi
events.desc: Timur's devastating invasion shakes the weakened Tughlaq empire, accelerating its decline.

events.title: End of the Tughlaq Dynasty
events.desc: The fragmented Tughlaq empire gives way to the Sayyid Dynasty.

people.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
people.note: r. 1325–1351; extended the empire to its greatest extent but is best known for bold, largely failed experiments.

people.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
people.note: r. 1351–1388; noted for welfare measures and public works.

people.name: Ziauddin Barani
people.note: Author of the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; wrote 'Kiran-us-Sa'dain'.

prelims: First dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate after the Khaljis; rule of four generations
Muhammad bin Tughlaq known for bold experiments (token currency, capital shift)
Firuz Shah Tughlaq known for welfare & public works; Timur's invasion (1398) marked the decline
mains: Tughlaq Dynasty was a time of experimentation and reforms
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's policies show both vision and challenges
Understanding this period is key to the decline of the Delhi Sultanate

quickFacts: Delhi (later Daulatabad during Muhammad bin Tughlaq)

periods.title: Sayyid Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Short-lived but Important Phase of Transition in the Delhi Sultanate
periods.overview: The first dynasty of the post-Tughlaq period, established by Khizr Khan (a Sayyid, appointed by Timur after his 1398 invasion). Rule strengthens briefly under Mubarak Shah before weakening under Muhammad Shah and collapsing into noble factionalism under the puppet ruler Alauddin Alam Shah, ending when Bahlul Lodi captures Delhi in 1451.

phases.name: Kizr Khan
points: Founder of the Sayyid Dynasty; appointed by Timur after his invasion (1398 CE)
Governor of Multan, later became Sultan of Delhi; tried to restore order and consolidated power
Established Sayyid Dynasty rule in Delhi in 1414 CE after Tughlaq decline

phases.name: Mubarak Shah
points: Most successful and capable ruler of the dynasty; reorganized administration and strengthened central authority
Controlled powerful nobles; encouraged agriculture; coins struck in his name
Relative stability and prosperity during his reign

phases.name: Muhammad Shah
points: Weak and ineffective ruler; administration fell into the hands of nobles
Rise of factionalism; royal authority declined; revolts by nobles and governors increased

phases.name: Alauddin Alam Shah
points: Puppet ruler in the hands of powerful nobles; real power rested with Khwaja Jahan (Wazir)
Central authority almost collapsed; decline of Sayyid power

phases.name: End of Sayyid Dynasty
points: Bahlul Lodi, a powerful Afghan noble, captured Delhi in 1451 CE and established Lodi rule, ending Sayyid rule

Political Administration: Kizr Khan: established Sayyid rule in Delhi, limited territory (mainly Delhi and surrounding areas), depended on old Tughlaq officials
Mubarak Shah: strengthened central administration, controlled powerful nobles, reorganized revenue collection
Muhammad Shah: lost control over nobles and provinces, factionalism increased, frequent revolts
Alauddin Alam Shah: no real power, controlled by nobles, Wazir Khwaja Jahan held real authority, administration in complete disorder
Economy: Kizr Khan: land revenue main source, agriculture slowly revived
Mubarak Shah: agriculture improved, trade and markets revived, currency system continued
Muhammad Shah: revenue system weakened, corruption increased
Alauddin Alam Shah: economic decline, irregular revenue collection, trade and agriculture affected
Religion: Ulama and Sufis remained influential across the dynasty; Islam remained the state religion; Persian language flourished in administration and literature

events.title: Kizr Khan founds the Sayyid Dynasty
events.desc: Establishes Sayyid rule in Delhi following the decline of the Tughlaqs, after being appointed by Timur.

events.title: Mubarak Shah's reign
events.desc: The most capable Sayyid ruler brings relative stability and prosperity through stronger administration.

events.title: Bahlul Lodi captures Delhi
events.desc: The Afghan noble Bahlul Lodi ends Sayyid rule and establishes the Lodi Dynasty.

people.name: Kizr Khan
people.note: r. 1414–1421; appointed by Timur.

people.name: Mubarak Shah
people.note: r. 1421–1434; most capable Sayyid ruler.

people.name: Khwaja Jahan
people.note: Held real authority during the reign of Alauddin Alam Shah.

prelims: First dynasty of the post-Tughlaq period; established by Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) with Turkish background
Limited control over territory and nobles; no strong rulers after Mubarak Shah
mains: Sayyid Dynasty was a phase of transition between Tughlaqs and Lodis
Power shifted from the crown to nobles and ministers
Laid the path for the rise of the Lodis and a new political order in North India

quickFacts: 1451 CE (Rise of Lodi Dynasty by Bahlul Lodi)

periods.title: Lodi Dynasty
periods.tagline: The Last Dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate — Political Instability, Regional Challenges and the Dawn of the Mughal Era
periods.overview: The last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, and the only Afghan (Pathan) dynasty to rule Delhi. Founded by Bahlul Lodi and consolidated by the able administrator Sikandar Lodi, the dynasty collapses under the harsh, alienating rule of Ibrahim Lodi, who is defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 — ending the Sultanate and beginning the Mughal era.

phases.name: Bahlul Lodi
points: Founder of the Lodi Dynasty; elected as Sultan by nobles; followed a policy of conciliation
Provincial governors enjoyed considerable autonomy; strengthened Afghan control in North India
Extended control over Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and parts of UP; maintained peace and won the trust of nobles

phases.name: Sikandar Lodi
points: Able and administrative ruler; centralized administration; reorganized provinces and appointed able officers
Reforms in revenue (Gaj-i-Sikandari land measurement), agriculture and market system; regulation of prices of commodities
Promoted learning, literature and Persian culture; founded Agra in 1504 CE; strict in religious matters

phases.name: Ibrahim Lodi
points: Last ruler of the Lodi Dynasty; highly centralised but in a harsh manner; ignored the advice of nobles
Arrogant and authoritarian; alienated nobles by his harsh attitude; many nobles revolted against him
Faced the external challenge of Babur's rise in Afghanistan; defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE)

phases.name: End of the Lodi Dynasty
points: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE)
Establishment of the Mughal Empire in India; end of Afghan rule in Delhi

Political Administration: Bahlul Lodi: elected as Sultan by nobles, followed policy of conciliation, provincial governors enjoyed autonomy, strengthened Afghan control in North India
Ibrahim Lodi: highly centralised but in a harsh manner, ignored advice of nobles, many nobles revolted against him, weak control over provinces
Economy: Bahlul Lodi: land revenue the main source, agriculture encouraged

Sikandar Lodi: revenue system improved and regularized, measurement of land (Gaj-i-Sikandari), irrigation works developed, regulation of prices of commodities, promoted agriculture and trade, concern for welfare of peasants
Ibrahim Lodi: economy weakened due to rebellions, heavy expenditure on army, weak revenue collection in provinces
Military: Bahlul Lodi: strong Afghan cavalry, maintained a disciplined army
Sikandar Lodi: well-organized army, modern weapons used, frontier protection strengthened
Ibrahim Lodi: large army but poorly loyal, nobles did not support him in war
Architecture & Culture: Bahlul Lodi: built many mosques and tombs (e.g. Bahlul Lodi's Tomb)
Sikandar Lodi: promoted Persian language and literature, patron of scholars like Mubarak Shah and Alam Khan, built many mosques, madrasas and gardens (e.g. Sikandar Lodi's Tomb, Lodi Gardens)
Ibrahim Lodi: no major architectural works

events.title: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi Dynasty
events.desc: The last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate is established after the decline of the Sayyids; Afghan power in North India is consolidated.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
events.desc: Sikandar Lodi's efficient administration, revenue reforms and cultural patronage mark the high point of Lodi rule.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire in India.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: r. 1489–1517; able administrator; founded Agra (1504).

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.note: r. 1517–1526; defeated and killed by Babur at Panipat.

prelims: Last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate; only Afghan (Pathan) dynasty to rule Delhi
Bahlul Lodi founded the dynasty in 1451 CE; Sikandar Lodi was an able administrator
Ended in 1526 CE with the defeat of Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat
mains: Ibrahim Lodi's misrule led to downfall; faced a growing external threat from Babur
Important for understanding the transition from Sultanate to Mughal rule

quickFacts: Delhi (later Agra founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1504)
1526 CE (Defeat by Babur in First Battle of Panipat)

periods.title: Vijayanagara Empire
periods.tagline: A Glorious Hindu Empire of South India — Defender of Dharma & Culture, Centre of Prosperity, Art, Literature and Trade
periods.overview: Founded at Hampi in 1336 CE as a bulwark against northern invasions, the Vijayanagara Empire passes through four dynasties — Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu — reaching its golden age of military success, prosperity, art and literature under Krishna Deva Raya, before the decisive defeat at the Battle of Talikota (1565) leads to the destruction of Hampi and a long, gradual decline.

phases.name: Foundation – Sangama Dynasty
points: Founded by Harihara I & Bukka Raya I in 1336 CE; capital Hampi (Vijayanagara)
Established a strong Hindu empire to protect dharma from invasions
Organized administration and built a powerful army; prosperity in agriculture, trade, art and literature

phases.name: Saluva Dynasty
points: Saluva Narasimha seized power in 1485; strengthened central authority
Continued expansion and administrative reforms; built new forts and tanks; encouraged art, literature and temple construction

phases.name: Tuluva Dynasty (Golden Age)
points: Founded by Vira Narasimha under guidance of Tuluva generals; greatest ruler Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529)
Empire reached its greatest extent; defeated Bahmani sultans, Gajapatis of Odisha and others
Age of prosperity, culture, literature and achievements

phases.name: Aravidu Dynasty
points: Capital shifted to Penukonda, later Chandragiri & Vellore; continued the legacy despite challenges
Faced pressure from the Deccan Sultanates; empire declined gradually

phases.name: End of Vijayanagara Empire
points: Defeated in the Battle of Talikota (1565 CE) by the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar)
Capital Hampi was destroyed and plundered; empire survived in reduced form under Aravidu rulers till 1646 CE

Political Administration: Sangama: well-organized administration, Nayaka system for provincial control, council of ministers and strong army
Saluva: centralized administration, reforms in revenue & military system, reduced power of old nobles
Tuluva: highly centralized & efficient administration, Amara-Nayaka system strengthened, strong espionage system, well organized army with cavalry, infantry, elephants & artillery
Aravidu: administration continued but weakened, power of Nayakas increased, frequent conflicts weakened central authority
Economy: Sangama: agriculture the main occupation, developed irrigation (tanks, canals), encouraged trade & crafts
Saluva: land revenue system improved, growth in trade (spices, horses, diamonds), state control on key commodities
Tuluva: prosperous economy, active foreign trade with Arabs, Persians, Portuguese, Chinese; export spices/textiles/precious stones, import horses/metals
Aravidu: economy affected by wars & invasions, decline in trade gradually, over-reliance on agriculture
Religion: Sangama: strong patronage to Hindu religion, reconstructed many temples, tolerant towards other religions
Tuluva: great supporter of Hinduism, built many grand temples (Vitthala, Hazara Rama), patronized saints & acharyas (Vyasa Tirtha), tolerant towards Islam & Christianity
Aravidu: continued temple patronage, growth of Bhakti movement, influence of saints & scholars continued
Art & Architecture: Sangama: built many temples, tanks & forts; Hampi became a beautiful city; blend of Dravidian & Indo-Islamic styles
Tuluva: golden age of architecture; Vitthala Temple, Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, Hazara Rama Temple; beautiful carvings, gopurams & sculptures
Aravidu: continued construction in smaller scale; temples at Tirupati, Srirangam, Kanchipuram

women.name: Queen Tirumalamba
women.note: Queen of Bukka Raya I; played an important role in royal and cultural activities.

women.name: Chinna Devi & Tirumala Devi
women.note: Queens of Krishna Deva Raya; helped in royal & cultural activities.

women.name: Women in society
women.note: Women were learned, respected & participated in religion, art, literature & social works; the Devadasi tradition supported art, music & dance.

events.title: Foundation of the Vijayanagara Empire
events.desc: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I found the empire at Hampi to protect dharma from northern invasions.

events.title: Reign of Krishna Deva Raya
events.desc: The empire's golden age: military success against the Bahmanis and Gajapatis, and a flowering of art, literature and architecture.

events.title: Battle of Talikota
events.desc: A coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeats Vijayanagara; the capital Hampi is destroyed and plundered.

events.title: End of the Vijayanagara Empire
events.desc: The empire, reduced to Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore under the Aravidu dynasty, finally ends.

people.name: Harihara I & Bukka Raya I
people.note: Founded the empire in 1336 CE.

people.name: Krishna Deva Raya
people.note: r. 1509–1529; empire reached its greatest extent under him.

prelims: First great Hindu empire of South India; capital Hampi (Vijayanagara)
Krishna Deva Raya – greatest ruler; ended after the Battle of Talikota (1565 CE)
Use of the Nayaka system for administration
mains: Vijayanagara Empire is a key example of a strong South Indian Hindu empire
Administration, economy, art & trade developed greatly under Krishna Deva Raya
Battle of Talikota (1565 CE) was the major turning point

periods.title: The Mughal Empire
periods.tagline: A Great Empire that Unified India — Pillars of Administration, Culture, Art & Architecture; a Symbol of Syncretic Culture and Prosperity
periods.overview: An overview of the Mughal Empire across seven great reigns — Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb, and the long Decline — tracing the empire's foundation at Panipat (1526), its consolidation and golden age under Akbar and Shah Jahan, its territorial overstretch under Aurangzeb, and its slow disintegration to the 1857 Revolt. Individual emperors are explored in full depth on their own dedicated pages.

phases.name: Babur
points: Founded the Mughal Empire in India after winning the Battle of Panipat (1526 CE); defeated Ibrahim Lodi
Battle of Khanwa (1527) and Ghaghra (1529); wrote 'Baburnama' (an autobiography); laid the foundation of a strong empire

phases.name: Humayun
points: Succeeded Babur; lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540); took refuge in Persia
Recovered Delhi in 1555; died in 1556 after a fall from the library stairs

phases.name: Akbar the Great
points: Greatest of the Mughals; expanded empire & consolidated rule; abolished Jizya & Pilgrimage Tax
Introduced Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace); Navaratnas in his court; reforms in administration, revenue, military & judiciary; promoted art, culture, literature & secularism

phases.name: Jahangir
points: Known for love of art & nature; strengthened administration; encouraged painting and naturalistic art
Wrote 'Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri' (memoirs); justice-loving ruler

phases.name: Shah Jahan
points: Golden age of Mughal architecture; built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Shalimar Gardens
Strong administration; empire at its territorial peak; luxurious court and culture

phases.name: Aurangzeb Alamgir
points: Last strong Mughal emperor; large territorial expansion; reimposed Jizya; long Deccan wars weakened the empire
Strict Sunni Muslim; death in 1707 marks the beginning of rapid decline

phases.name: Decline
points: Weak successors; power struggle among Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Rohillas & regional states
Economic decline; British East India Company became dominant; last Mughal Bahadur Shah II; 1857: end of Mughal rule

Political Administration: Babur: centralised rule, divided empire into provinces, trusted nobles
Akbar: efficient central administration, Mansabdari system, Subah-Sarkar-Pargana system, record keeping
Jahangir: continued Akbar's system, strong bureaucracy, imperial authority at its peak
Shah Jahan: highly centralised, increased control but more dependence on nobles
Aurangzeb: centralisation continued but weakened later
Economy: Babur: booty from victories, agriculture encouraged
Akbar: land revenue system (Zabt), Todar Mal's bandobast, promotion of trade & crafts
Jahangir: trade & industry flourished, expansion of markets, increase in revenue
Shah Jahan: prosperity & wealth high, growth of handicrafts, textiles, trade
Aurangzeb: heavy expenditure on wars, economic strain, decline in trade in later period
Religion: Akbar: policy of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace), abolished Jizya, Din-i-Ilahi
Jahangir & Shah Jahan: generally tolerant, followed policies broadly similar to Akbar
Aurangzeb: reimposed Jizya, orthodox Sunni ruler
Art, Architecture & Culture: Akbar: blend of Indian, Persian & Central Asian styles, Fatehpur Sikri, Agra Fort
Jahangir: painting at its best, naturalistic art
Shah Jahan: golden age of architecture — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid
Aurangzeb: less focus on art & architecture

women.name: Nur Jahan
women.note: Influential queen during Jahangir's reign; involved in administration, coinage, architecture & charity work.

women.name: Jahanara Begum
women.note: Daughter of Shah Jahan; patron of arts, built 'Sarais', involved in trade & welfare.

women.name: Zeb-un-Nissa
women.note: Scholar, poetess (wrote in Persian); daughter of Aurangzeb.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire in India.

events.title: Akbar's accession
events.desc: Akbar becomes emperor at age 13 and goes on to consolidate and expand the empire into its golden age.

events.title: Aurangzeb's reign
events.desc: The empire reaches its greatest territorial extent but is weakened by prolonged Deccan wars and reimposed Jizya.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline amid weak successors and regional power struggles.

events.title: End of Mughal rule
events.desc: The Revolt of 1857 and its suppression bring a formal end to Mughal rule in India.

people.name: Shah Jahan
people.note: r. 1628–1658; builder of the Taj Mahal.

prelims: Founder: Babur (1526); Greatest Emperor: Akbar; Duration: 1526–1857 CE (331 years)
Dynasty: Timurid (Mughal); Capital(s): Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, Delhi, Shahjahanabad
End: 1857 Revolt – End of Mughal Rule
mains: Mughal Empire brought political stability and administrative efficiency
Akbar's policies were the turning point for unity and secularism
Mughal era is the golden age of Indian art, architecture & culture
Understanding the decline of the Mughals is key to the British rise in India

quickFacts: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, Delhi, Shahjahanabad

periods.title: Babur
periods.tagline: The First Mughal Emperor — A Timurid Prince, Warrior, Writer and Visionary
periods.overview: Babur, a Timurid prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, spent years in exile after losing Farghana before being invited to India by discontented Afghan nobles. His victory at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and subsequent battles at Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529) established the Mughal Empire, which he ruled for four brief but foundational years before his death in 1530.

phases.name: Early Life & Background
points: Born 14 February 1483 in Andijan (Fergana Valley, present-day Uzbekistan); great-great-grandson of Timur (Tamerlane) and Genghis Khan
Lost his father at a young age; became ruler of Farghana at age 12; lost Samarkand several times but gained rich experience in wars and administration; spent years in exile

phases.name: Invasion of India
points: Invited by Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan (discontented nobles of the Delhi Sultanate) to fight Ibrahim Lodi
Crossed the Indus in November 1524 with an army of about 12,000–15,000; reached Punjab, captured Lahore (1524) and Dipalpur; advanced towards Delhi

phases.name: First Battle of Panipat
points: Faced Ibrahim Lodi's army (about 100,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants)
Babur used superior strategy: Tulughma (flanking attack), Araba (cart fortification), matchlocks & artillery
Ibrahim Lodi was killed; Babur won a historic victory and captured Delhi & Agra

phases.name: Conquest & Control
points: Captured Delhi (April 1526) and Agra (May 1526)
Defeated Rajput ruler Rana Sanga of Mewar in the Battle of Khanwa (16 March 1527)
Defeated Afghan chiefs Mahmud Lodi in the Battle of Chanderi (1528) and the Afghan confederacy in the Battle of Ghaghra (1529); established firm control over North India

phases.name: Last Years & Death
points: Spent his last years consolidating his rule; died on 26 December 1530 in Agra at the age of 47
Buried in Aram Bagh, Agra (his own garden)

Administration: Personal rule; no elaborate bureaucracy like later Mughals; advisors and military commanders helped in governance
Divided the empire into provinces (subahs) and smaller units; appointed governors (khalifas) and officials
Followed Islamic principles and Timurid traditions in justice; maintained a standing army and loyal Turkish-Mongol cavalry
Economy: No formal revenue system; relied on land revenue and personal control
Supported farming and encouraged irrigation in key regions; connected India with Central Asia and beyond through trade routes
Continued the use of existing coins; issued coins in his name in later years
Military: Central Asian style of warfare (cavalry, archers, matchlocks); used artillery and firearms (advanced for his time)
Strategic use of war elephants and cavalry; the Tulughma (flanking movement) and Araba (cart fortification) systems were decisive at Panipat and Khanwa
Culture & Intellectual Life: A learned and literary emperor; wrote the 'Baburnama' (autobiography) in Chagatai Turkish (later translated into Persian and English)
Patronized Persian and Central Asian scholars, poets and artists; introduced Persianate culture and traditions in India
Loved gardens, nature, poetry and calligraphy; laid the foundation for the Mughal artistic tradition; introduced the Charbagh style of garden architecture (e.g. Aram Bagh in Lahore)

women.name: Qutlugh Nigar Khanum
women.note: Played a significant role in his life and court; well-educated and supported literary and cultural activities. Though her direct political role was limited, her presence strengthened the royal household and cultural environment.

events.title: Birth of Babur
events.desc: Born in Andijan; descended from Timur and Genghis Khan through the Chagatai line.

events.title: Invasion of India
events.desc: Invited by discontented Afghan nobles, Babur advances from Kabul via Panipat, capturing Lahore and Punjab.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi using the Tulughma flanking tactic, artillery and cart fortifications, founding the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Battle of Khanwa
events.desc: Babur defeats the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar, securing Mughal control of North India.

events.title: Battles of Chanderi and Ghaghra
events.desc: Babur defeats the Afghan chief Mahmud Lodi and an Afghan confederacy, consolidating control over North India.

events.title: Death of Babur
events.desc: Babur dies in Agra; succeeded by his son Humayun.

people.name: Babur
people.note: r. 1526–1530; author of the Baburnama.

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.role: Last Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate
people.note: Defeated and killed by Babur at Panipat, 1526.

people.name: Rana Sanga
people.note: Defeated by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa, 1527.

prelims: First Mughal emperor to establish rule in India; founder of the Mughal Dynasty
Wrote the Baburnama — a valuable historical source; introduced modern warfare techniques (gunpowder, artillery, Tulughma, Araba)
Major battles: Panipat (1526), Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528), Ghaghra (1529)
mains: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and established the Mughal Empire
He was not just a conqueror but a visionary who laid the foundation of one of the greatest empires in Indian history
His works (Baburnama) remain valuable sources of history, culture and society of the time

periods.title: Humayun
periods.tagline: The Second Mughal Emperor — Restorer of the Empire, Patron of Culture, Learning & Architecture
periods.overview: Humayun succeeded Babur in 1530 but lost his empire to Sher Shah Suri after defeats at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), spending fifteen years in exile in Persia. With Safavid military support he defeated the Suri successors and recaptured Delhi in 1555, restoring Mughal rule shortly before his death in 1556 — a reign whose greatest legacy was perseverance, and paving the way for Akbar's golden age.

phases.name: Accession & Early Years
points: Became emperor after Babur's death on 26 December 1530; faced challenges from his brothers (Kamran, Askari, Hindal); spent initial years securing the empire

phases.name: Challenges & Loss of Empire
points: Strong Afghan challenge under Sher Shah Suri; defeated at Chausa (1539); defeated at Kannauj/Bilgram (1540); lost Delhi & Agra, went into exile

phases.name: Exile & Persian Years
points: Took refuge in Sindh, Rajasthan and finally Persia; received help from Shah Tahmasp I of Iran; stayed in Persia for about 15 years, learning Persian culture, Shia ideas, art, etiquette and administration

phases.name: Reconquest of India
points: With Persian military support, returned to India; defeated Sikandar Suri at Machhiwara (Punjab) in 1555; recaptured Delhi (23 July 1555) and Agra; gradually restored Mughal rule in North India

phases.name: Last Years & Death
points: Spent last year consolidating his rule; died on 24 January 1556 in Delhi after a fall from the stairs of his library at Purana Qila; buried in Humayun's Tomb, Delhi (first garden-tomb in India)

Political Administration: Tried to maintain his father Babur's administrative system; appointed competent nobles in provinces; could not centralise authority strongly due to constant struggles
Economy: Revenue system continued as before; encouraged trade and commerce; promoted agriculture, dug canals and restored wells in some areas
Military: Inherited a strong army from Babur; used artillery and firearms; defeats due to Afghan strategy and lack of stability; reorganized the army with Persian help during exile
Art, Architecture & Culture: Great patron of Persian culture, literature, art and architecture; introduced Persian artists, calligraphers and scholars in India
Built Humayun's Tomb in Delhi (designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas) — first garden tomb in India; loved books and astrology; established a large library at Purana Qila
Foreign Relations: Good relations with Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I of Persia; received military and financial help during exile

women.name: Haji Begum (Humayun's sister)
women.note: Played a key role during the crisis; managed affairs and supported Humayun in exile.

women.name: Gulbadan Begum
women.note: Wrote the Humayun-nama, an important primary source for this period.

events.title: Humayun's accession
events.desc: Succeeds Babur as the second Mughal emperor, immediately facing challenges from his brothers.

events.title: Defeats at Chausa and Kannauj
events.desc: Sher Shah Suri decisively defeats Humayun, who loses Delhi and Agra and goes into exile.

events.title: Persian exile
events.desc: Humayun spends fifteen years in exile, receiving refuge and military support from the Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I.

events.title: Reconquest of Delhi
events.desc: With Persian support, Humayun defeats the Suri successors and recaptures Delhi and Agra, restoring Mughal rule.

events.title: Death of Humayun
events.desc: Humayun dies after a fall from his library stairs at Purana Qila; his son Akbar becomes emperor at age 13.

people.name: Sher Shah Suri
people.note: Defeated Humayun and ruled North India 1540–1545.

people.name: Shah Tahmasp I
people.note: Provided refuge and military support to Humayun in exile.

prelims: Second Mughal Emperor of India; lost his empire to Sher Shah Suri but restored it in 1555
Built Humayun's Tomb — first garden-tomb in India; spent 15 years in exile in Persia
mains: Humayun's life teaches perseverance and patience — he lost his empire but regained it through hard work and learning
Highlights the importance of foreign relations (Persia); his restoration paved the way for Akbar's golden age

quickFacts: 24 January 1556, Delhi; buried in Humayun's Tomb

periods.title: The Sur Interregnum
periods.tagline: A Turbulent Decade and a Half that Saw the Decline of the Sur Empire and the Re-emergence of the Mughals under Humayun
periods.overview: Between Humayun's two reigns, Sher Shah Suri occupies Delhi and founds the Sur Empire, introducing a model administrative, revenue and communication system that later Mughal rulers would build on. His son Islam Shah Suri continues consolidation, but factionalism among weak successors after 1553 fatally weakens the Sur state, allowing Humayun to recapture Delhi in 1555.

phases.name: Sher Shah Suri
points: Occupied Delhi in 1540 after defeating Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540); founded the Sur Empire
Able and just ruler; died on 22 May 1545 (accidental death)

phases.name: Islam Shah Suri
points: Succeeded Sher Shah; expanded & consolidated the empire; efficient administrator; died on 19 November 1553 (natural death)

phases.name: Internal Struggles
points: Weak successors led to factionalism — Adil Shah, Ibrahim Shah, Sikandar Shah and others; nobles fought for power; empire lost strength

phases.name: Humayun's Return
points: Took advantage of Sur disunity; with help of Persian Shah Tahmasp, re-entered Delhi on 23 July 1555; re-established Mughal rule

phases.name: Humayun's Death
points: Died on 24 January 1556 after falling from the stairs of his library at Purana Qila, Delhi; Akbar became emperor at age 13

Political Administration: Sher Shah: established the Sur Empire, strong central authority, divided the empire into provinces (Sarkars) and districts (Parganas)
Islam Shah: consolidated the empire, maintained law & order, efficient bureaucracy
Period of instability (1553–1555): weak rulers, factionalism among nobles, loss of central control
Economy: Sher Shah: land revenue system (Zabt), measurement of land, fixed revenue demand
Islam Shah: continued revenue reforms, encouraged agriculture, trade & industry
Instability period: revenue system neglected, jagirdars became powerful, economic decline
Administration & Infrastructure: Sher Shah built roads (e.g. Grand Trunk Road, Sonargaon to Peshawar), constructed sarais at regular intervals, improved communications, introduced standard weights and measures, a well-organized postal system (Dak Chowkis), Patta (record of rights) & Qabuliyat (agreement)

women.name: Women in this period
women.note: Very little direct mention of prominent women in the sources for the Sur period; women generally lived in purdah; the era was comparatively peaceful under Sher Shah and Islam Shah.

events.title: Sher Shah Suri founds the Sur Empire
events.desc: After defeating Humayun at Chausa and Kannauj, Sher Shah occupies Delhi and establishes efficient, model administration.

events.title: Sher Shah's administrative reforms
events.desc: Construction of the Grand Trunk Road, a standardized revenue system, and a postal network become a model later adopted by the Mughals.

events.title: Sur factionalism
events.desc: Weak successors after Islam Shah's death lead to noble infighting and the collapse of central control.

events.title: Humayun recaptures Delhi
events.desc: Taking advantage of Sur disunity, and with Persian support, Humayun re-enters Delhi, ending the Sur Interregnum.

people.name: Sher Shah Suri
people.note: r. 1540–1545; model of good governance.

people.name: Islam Shah Suri
people.note: r. 1545–1553; consolidator.

prelims: Sher Shah Suri = Model of Good Governance; Islam Shah Suri = Consolidator
Weak successors after 1553 led to decline; Humayun's return in 1555 ended the Sur Interregnum
mains: Shows how good governance strengthened a state, and its decline through internal disunity
A transition phase to the rise of Akbar; efficient land revenue system became a model for the later Mughals

quickFacts: Chausa (1539), Kannauj (1540), Death of Sher Shah (1545), Death of Islam Shah (1553), Humayun's Return (1555)

periods.title: Akbar the Great
periods.tagline: Founder of a United & Tolerant India — Builder of Empire, Promoter of Unity, Patron of Culture, Pioneer of Good Governance
periods.overview: Becoming emperor at 13 after Humayun's death, Akbar moved from Bairam Khan's regency through consolidation, sweeping territorial expansion, and landmark administrative and religious reforms — including the Mansabdari system, the Zabt/Dahsala revenue system, abolition of Jizya, and the policy of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace) — to build the Mughal Empire's most enduring foundations and preside over what is widely regarded as its Golden Age.

phases.name: Accession
points: Became emperor at the age of 13 after Humayun's death; Bairam Khan acted as regent; defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556)

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Captured Delhi & Agra; eliminated threats from Sikandar Sur (1557) and other Afghan chieftains; made Bairam Khan retire (1560); started direct rule

phases.name: Expansion
points: Conquered Malwa (1561), Gujarat (1572), Bengal (1576), Rajasthan/Amber (1562), Marwar (1568), Bikaner/Jaisalmer (1570), Sindh (1591), Kashmir (1586)
Defeated Mughals in Kabul & Qandahar (1581); annexed vast new territories

phases.name: Administrative & Ideological Innovations
points: Introduced Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace); abolished Jizya (1564); started Din-i-Ilahi (1582)
Regularized administration and revenue system (Dahsala system by Todar Mal); strengthened central authority

phases.name: Last Years
points: Consolidated empire and ensured stability; patronized art, culture, literature and learning; died on 27 October 1605 at Agra

Political Administration: Established centralized administration; Mansabdari System (graded ranking of nobles, 10 to 10,000); Jagirdari System (land assignments in lieu of salary)
Abolished the practice of transferring jagirs in revenue-rich areas only; established an efficient intelligence system; improved provincial administration — Subah, Sarkar, Pargana system
Economy: Land Revenue System – Dahsala System (introduced by Todar Mal); measurement of land – Zabt System; classification of land and crops; fixed revenue demand – 1/3rd of average produce
Encouraged agriculture, irrigation, trade and crafts; developed infrastructure — roads, sarais, bridges
Religion: Policy of Sulh-i-Kul – peace with all; abolished Jizya (1564) and Pilgrimage Tax; held Ibadat Khana discussions (from 1575) with scholars of different religions
Promoted Sulh (ethical monotheism); established Din-i-Ilahi (1582) — a spiritual path based on truth, morality and service
Society: Promoted social harmony and integration; abolished slavery (except prisoners of war); encouraged inter-caste and inter-faith relations
Rajput policy — matrimonial alliances, high positions for Rajputs; won hearts of people through justice and welfare measures
Art, Architecture & Learning: Blended Indian, Persian and Central Asian styles; built Fatehpur Sikri, Agra Fort (renovated), Lahore Fort; patronized miniature painting — Mughal School of Painting
Encouraged literature in Persian, Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic; translated the Mahabharata (Razmnama), Ramayana, Atharvaveda, Upanishads, Bible etc. into Persian; founded Maktabs and Madrasas

women.name: Mariam-uz-Zamani (Harkha Bai)
women.note: Hindu Rajput princess; influential in court, patron of charity & trade activities.

women.name: Salima Sultan Begum
women.note: Daughter of Sher Shah; author of the Humayun-nama; respected by Akbar.

women.name: Ruqaiya Sultan Begum
women.note: Educated and cultured; maintained correspondence.

women.name: Jodha Bai (Harkha Bai)
women.note: Akbar's chief consort; promoted religious harmony.

women.name: Other royal women
women.note: Played important roles in administration, charity, diplomacy and cultural patronage; though women did not hold formal political power, they had significant influence in court & society.

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat
events.desc: The young Akbar, guided by Bairam Khan, defeats Hemu and secures the throne.

events.title: Abolition of Jizya
events.desc: Akbar abolishes the Jizya tax on non-Muslims, part of his broader policy of religious tolerance.

events.title: Conquest of Gujarat and Bengal
events.desc: Major territorial expansion consolidates Mughal control over key trading regions.

events.title: Ibadat Khana established
events.desc: A 'House of Worship' at Fatehpur Sikri where Akbar holds interfaith religious discussions.

events.title: Din-i-Ilahi founded
events.desc: Akbar introduces a spiritual path for a select few followers, based on truth, morality and service — never a state religion.

events.title: Death of Akbar
events.desc: Akbar dies at Agra, leaving behind a strong, stable and inclusive empire.

people.name: Akbar the Great
people.note: r. 1556–1605; widely regarded as the greatest Mughal emperor.

people.name: Bairam Khan
people.note: Guided the young Akbar through the empire's early consolidation.

people.name: Raja Todar Mal
people.note: Devised the Dahsala/Zabt land revenue system.

people.name: Abul Fazl
people.note: Author of the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari.

prelims: Akbar's reign is often called the Golden Age of the Mughal Empire
Mansabdari System, Dahsala Revenue System, Zabt System, Sulh-i-Kul, Din-i-Ilahi
Abolished Jizya (1564) and the Pilgrimage Tax; caution — Din-i-Ilahi was a spiritual path for a select few, not a state religion
mains: Represents ideal governance and secularism; important for Polity (Administration), Economy, Society, Culture, Religion, Art & Architecture
His administrative and revenue reforms ensured stability and prosperity; he promoted a composite culture that is the foundation of India's unity in diversity

quickFacts: Second Battle of Panipat (1556), Gujarat (1572), Haldighati (1576)*

periods.title: Jahangir
periods.tagline: The Fourth Mughal Emperor — Connoisseur of Art & Nature, Just and Tolerant Ruler
periods.overview: Jahangir continues Akbar's administrative and religious-tolerance policies through a reign notable for justice reforms (the Chain of Justice), the flourishing of naturalistic Mughal painting, the growing influence of his powerful and capable wife Nur Jahan, and expanding contact with Europe, including the 1615–1619 embassy of Sir Thomas Roe and a 1608 trading charter to the English East India Company.

phases.name: Accession
points: Acceded to the throne on 24 October 1605 after the death of Akbar; faced rebellion of his son Khusrau (1606 CE) which was suppressed; married Jagat Gosain (1607), daughter of Raja Man Singh

phases.name: Consolidation & Early Years
points: Consolidated the empire and continued Akbar's policies; strengthened nobility through the Mansabdari system; patronised arts, culture and literature

phases.name: Major Events & Developments
points: Granted a charter to the English East India Company (1608) to establish a factory at Surat; Prince Khusrau rebelled again (1612) but was defeated and blinded
Nur Jahan became a powerful influence after their marriage (1611); Jahangir invaded Kangra (1615) and incorporated it; Sir Thomas Roe, English ambassador, visited the court (1615–19)

phases.name: Later Years
points: Spent more time in pleasure, art and nature; continued peace and prosperity in the empire; administration remained efficient though with increasing influence of the Nur Jahan group

phases.name: Death
points: Died on 28 October 1627 at Lahore; succeeded by his son Shah Jahan; buried in Shahdara (Lahore) in a magnificent tomb

Political Administration: Maintained strong central authority and the mansabdari system; efficient revenue administration continued; emphasis on justice and welfare of subjects
Justice & Reforms: Introduced the 'Chain of Justice' to ensure people could directly appeal to the king; appointment of able ministers and officials; continued land revenue system and mansabdari system; focus on welfare of subjects and fair taxation
Religion: Followed the policy of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace) of Akbar; personally inclined towards Sufism; promoted tolerance and religious harmony
Art, Architecture & Culture: Flourishing of Mughal painting; naturalism and portraiture reached its peak; development of gardens (Shalimar Bagh, Kashmir); patronised literature in Persian; wrote the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (autobiography)
Foreign Relations: Friendly relations with England; charter to the English East India Company (1608); contacts with Persia, Ottoman Empire, Europe; Sir Thomas Roe's embassy (1615–19) was an important event

women.name: Nur Jahan (Mehr-un-Nisa)
women.note: Exercised great influence on administration, politics and military decisions; issued farmans in her own name; patron of arts, architecture and culture.

women.name: Jagat Gosain
women.note: Wife of Jahangir; other women also influenced court culture.

events.title: Jahangir's accession
events.desc: Ascends the throne after Akbar's death and continues most of his father's policies.

events.title: Rebellions of Prince Khusrau
events.desc: Jahangir's son rebels twice; the second rebellion ends with Khusrau's defeat and blinding.

events.title: Charter to the English East India Company
events.desc: Jahangir grants trading rights, allowing the English to establish a factory at Surat.

periods.title: Shah Jahan
periods.tagline: The Patron of Architecture & Culture — Great Builder, Strong Administrator, Cultural Zenith of the Mughals
periods.overview: Shah Jahan's reign marks the territorial and cultural peak of the Mughal Empire: strong centralized administration, major military campaigns (Bundelkhand, Mewar, the Deccan, Qandahar, Assam), moderate religious policy, and an unmatched architectural legacy — the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Shahjahanabad — before a war of succession among his sons (1657–58) ends with his deposition and imprisonment by Aurangzeb.

phases.name: Accession & Consolidation
points: Ascends the throne on 8 February 1628 after the death of Jahangir; consolidation of power; submission of rivals; marriage with Arjumand Banu Begum (Mumtaz Mahal) had occurred in 1612, formal reign begins 1628

phases.name: Military Campaigns & Expansion
points: Campaign in Bundelkhand (1632); suppression of revolt of Hindu Rao in Mewar (1635); conquest of Qandahar (1636, lost again in 1639 to Safavids)
Conflict with the Portuguese at Surat and Daman (1644–45); revolt in Deccan by Qutb Shahi ruler (1645–46); war with the Ahoms of Assam (1652–53)

phases.name: Cultural Zenith
points: Strengthening of administration and empire; economic prosperity; art, culture & architecture patronage reaches its peak — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Shahjahanabad, Shalimar Gardens

phases.name: War of Succession & Decline
points: Illness of Shah Jahan (1657) triggers a war of succession among his sons; defeat and imprisonment of Shah Jahan by Aurangzeb (1658); lived in Agra Fort till his death

phases.name: Death
points: Died in 1666 in Agra Fort; buried in the Taj Mahal, Agra, alongside Mumtaz Mahal

Political Administration: Absolute monarchy with divine right theory; strong central authority and efficient bureaucracy; Mansabdari System further regularised (ranks between 10 and 7,000)

Provincial administration: Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → Village; 17 (later 18) Subahs during his reign; revenue administration based on Todar Mal's system of measurement, Zabt (cash assessment) and Kankut
Economy: Agriculture the mainstay of the economy; Zabt system of Todar Mal continued; other revenues — Jizya (on non-Muslims), customs, transit duties, tribute, fines
Irrigation — construction of canals, tanks and wells; trade & commerce flourished, both internal & external; industries & crafts — textiles (cotton, silk), metalware, carpets, paper, glass, jewellery
Ports: Surat, Masulipatnam, Hugli, Thatta; English, Dutch, French, Portuguese companies active in trade; prosperity due to peace, good administration and flourishing trade
Religion: Personally a devout Sunni Muslim; patronised Islamic scholars and jurists; endowed madrasas, mosques and religious institutions

Did not reimpose Jizya (which was abolished by Akbar); no general ban on temples — many were built and numerous Hindu institutions received grants; promoted an atmosphere of tolerance and justice, though following a moderate (not fully liberal) policy compared to Akbar
Architecture & Cultural Achievements: Known as the 'Patron of Architecture'; use of white marble, pietra dura inlay, symmetry and grandeur; Taj Mahal, Red Fort (Delhi), Jama Masjid (Delhi), Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi)

Other buildings: Moti Masjid (Agra), Diwan-i-Khas (Delhi), Shalimar Gardens (Lahore), Masjid-i-Wazir Khan (Lahore); literature, music, painting and calligraphy flourished; court life reached its zenith

people.name: Shah Jahan

people.name: Mumtaz Mahal

Did not reimpose Jizya; empire reached its greatest territorial extent during his reign
Caution: do not assume Shah Jahan was completely liberal or orthodox; his policy was practical and state-focused
mains: Understand Shah Jahan as the builder-king who brought cultural splendour, administrative efficiency and prosperity, but whose lavish spending and political tensions created challenges for the future
War of Succession (1657–58) weakened the empire and paved the way for Aurangzeb's challenges

quickFacts: 1666, Agra Fort; buried in the Taj Mahal

periods.title: Aurangzeb Alamgir
periods.tagline: The Last Great Mughal Emperor — Expansion, Centralisation, Religious Policy, Deccan Wars, and the Causes of Decline
periods.overview: Aurangzeb wins a bitter war of succession, executing his brother Dara Shikoh and imprisoning Shah Jahan, then rules for 49 years, expanding the empire to its greatest territorial extent through prolonged Deccan campaigns against Bijapur, Golconda and the rising Marathas. His reimposition of Jizya (1679) and orthodox religious policy, combined with jagirdari crisis and administrative overstretch, are widely identified as key causes of the empire's subsequent decline.

phases.name: War of Succession & Accession
points: War of succession among Shah Jahan's sons; Battle of Dharmat (April 1658), Battle of Samugarh (29 May 1658); defeat and imprisonment of Shah Jahan in Agra Fort
Battle of Khajwa (Jan 1659) against Shah Shuja; execution of Dara Shikoh (Aug 1659); Aurangzeb assumes undisputed control (1659)

phases.name: Consolidation & Deccan Campaigns
points: Deccan and frontier campaigns; 1663 – attack by Shivaji on Shaista Khan at Pune; 1665 – Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji; 1666 – Shivaji's visit to Agra and daring escape
1670s – rise of Maratha resistance in Western Deccan; 1675 – execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur; 1679 – reimposition of Jizya on non-Muslims

phases.name: Rajput & Sikh Conflicts, Rise of the Marathas
points: Rajput conflicts (especially Mewar and Marwar); 1681 – Aurangzeb moves to the Deccan permanently; 1686 – conquest of Bijapur; 1687 – conquest of Golconda
1689 – capture and execution of Sambhaji; prolonged Deccan wars against the Marathas continue through the 1690s

phases.name: Decline & Death
points: Expansion to its greatest territorial extent but resources exhausted; Marathas became stronger; regional resistance and fragmentation of Mughal power
Death of Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar (3 March 1707), buried at Khuldabad, Maharashtra in a simple grave as per his wishes

Political & Administrative System: Centralised monarchy — absolute authority of the emperor; Mansabdari system (ranks of 10 to 70,000) combining military & administrative responsibilities
Jagirdari system (land grants as salary to mansabdars); provincial administration: Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → Village; increasing jagirdari pressure led to a jagirdari crisis
Administrative overstretch due to long Deccan wars; intelligence system of Barid (spies) and news-writers
Economy: Agriculture the backbone of the economy; land revenue the main source of state income; Zabt system (Dahsala system of Akbar continued with modifications)
Heavy expenditure on continuous wars and military campaigns; economic consequences — decline in agrarian conditions in some regions, jagirdari crisis, peasant burdens increased
Religious Policy: Personal Sunni orthodoxy; observed Islamic practices strictly; patronage to Islamic scholars, ulema and madrasas

Fatawa-i-Alamgiri — compilation of Islamic law; reimposition of Jizya in 1679 on non-Muslims; restrictions on some religious practices, festivals, and building of new temples in specific contexts (not a uniform empire-wide policy)

UPSC caution: avoid the simplistic statement that Aurangzeb completely removed all Hindu officials or destroyed all temples — his policies varied by region, political context and period; historians debate whether his actions were political/situational or uniformly anti-Hindu
Military & Deccan Policy: Large standing army with huge numbers of cavalry; strong artillery & use of firearms; fort warfare — Mughals strong in capturing and maintaining forts
Strengths: resources, artillery, organised administration, large manpower; weaknesses: heavy expenditure, slow movement in Deccan, rigid system against fast, local-support Maratha guerrilla warfare
Relation with the Marathas: Rise of Shivaji and consolidation of Maratha power (1645–1680); Treaty of Purandar (1665); Shivaji's coronation at Raigad (1674)

Maratha resistance expands under Shivaji's successors; Aurangzeb personally leads Deccan campaigns from 1681 onward; long-term impact — Marathas emerge as a major power, Mughal control weakens in the Deccan and beyond

women.name: Zeb-un-Nissa
women.note: Daughter of Aurangzeb (1639–1702); scholar, poet (pen name 'Makfi'); well-educated in Persian, Arabic and literature.

women.name: Zinat-un-Nissa Begum
women.note: Known for charity, held political influence and supported religious institutions.

women.name: Women of the Royal Household
women.note: Patronage of mosques, sarais, gardens and charitable works; influence in politics and court life during early Aurangzeb period.

events.title: War of Succession
events.desc: Aurangzeb defeats his brothers in a bitter succession struggle and imprisons Shah Jahan.

events.title: Reimposition of Jizya
events.desc: Aurangzeb reimposes the tax on non-Muslims, abolished decades earlier by Akbar, a defining and controversial policy shift.

events.title: Conquest of Bijapur and Golconda
events.desc: Aurangzeb annexes the last major Deccan sultanates, extending the empire to its greatest territorial extent.

events.title: Execution of Sambhaji
events.desc: The Maratha leader Sambhaji is captured and executed, but Maratha resistance continues under his successors.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Dies at Ahmadnagar after prolonged Deccan wars; his death marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline.

people.name: Aurangzeb (Alamgir)
people.note: r. 1658–1707; 'Conqueror of the World'.

people.name: Dara Shikoh
people.note: Executed by Aurangzeb in 1659.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Chief Deccan adversary; challenged Mughal authority.

people.name: Sambhaji
people.note: Son of Shivaji; captured and executed by Aurangzeb in 1689.

prelims: Longest-reigning Mughal emperor (49 years); title Alamgir; reimposed Jizya in 1679
Major opponents: Marathas, Rajputs, Sikhs, Deccan states; conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)
mains: Aurangzeb expanded the empire to its greatest extent but sowed the seeds of its decline
Causes of decline: prolonged Deccan wars, jagirdari crisis, high military expenditure, religious policies, rise of regional powers, administrative overstretch
Historians debate whether his religious policy was uniformly anti-Hindu or shaped by political and situational context — analyse policies in their historical context and avoid extreme judgement

quickFacts: 3 March 1707, Ahmadnagar; buried at Khuldabad, Maharashtra

periods.title: Later Mughal Empire
periods.tagline: From Aurangzeb's Death to the End of Mughal Rule in India — Decline of Central Authority, Regionalisation, Economic Strain, European Intervention
periods.overview: Following Aurangzeb's death in 1707, a rapid succession of weak emperors preside over the collapse of central Mughal authority: the jagirdari crisis, peasant and zamindar discontent, and devastating external invasions (Nadir Shah 1739, Ahmad Shah Abdali's five invasions) accelerate the rise of regional powers — the Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Rohillas and independent Nawabs — while the English East India Company steadily gains political and revenue control, culminating in the 1857 Revolt and the formal end of Mughal rule in 1858.

phases.name: Aurangzeb's Death & War of Succession
points: Death of Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar (3 March 1707); war of succession among his sons; Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam) becomes emperor — an able soldier but faces the Marathas & Sikhs

phases.name: Rapid Succession of Weak Emperors
points: Jahandar Shah (1712–13) – indulgent, short reign; Farrukhsiyar (1713–19) – increased influence of the Sayyid Brothers; Rafi-ud-Darajat & Rafi-ud-Daula (1719–1727) – weak, figurehead rulers
Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' (1727–1748) – cultural patronage but weak politically; Nadir Shah invades India and sacks Delhi (March 1739)

phases.name: Rise of Regional Powers
points: Ahmad Shah Abdali's invasions (5 major invasions, 1740–1754); Battle of Plassey (1757) and Battle of Buxar (1764) establish British political power
Diwani rights granted to the English East India Company (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) in 1765

phases.name: Mughal Emperor as a Puppet
points: Shah Alam II under nominal, then British, control (1772–1806); Delhi occupied by Lord Lake (1803); Akbar Shah II under British control (1806–1837)

phases.name: Revolt of 1857 & End of Mughal Rule
points: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), the last Mughal, becomes a symbol of the Revolt of 1857 (the First War of Independence)
Deposition of Bahadur Shah II (Sept 1857); end of Mughal rule and beginning of British Crown rule (1858)

Political & Administrative System: Central authority declined sharply; emperors became figureheads; real power passed to nobles, court factions and provincial governors
Mansabdari & Jagirdari systems collapsed gradually; increase in jagirdari crisis — jagirs became insufficient and unpaid
Provincial governors became independent — Nizam (Hyderabad), Nawabs (Bengal, Awadh), Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Rohillas; factions at court — Irani, Turani, Hindustani, Deccani, Sayyid Brothers
Economy: Agriculture remained the mainstay; land revenue system in decline; heavy exactions by jagirdars, zamindars and intermediaries

Jagirdari crisis led to revenue farming and corruption; trade and commerce declined in inland regions; crafts and industries suffered due to instability, invasions and competition with Europeans; Company gained Diwani (1765) — financial control over rich provinces
External Invasions: 1739: Nadir Shah invaded, defeated the Mughals at Karnal, sacked Delhi, took the Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne
1748–1757: Ahmad Shah Abdali's repeated invasions (five in total); caused immense destruction, loss of prestige, wealth and control; encouraged regional powers to assert independence
Rise of Regional Powers: Marathas emerged as the strongest power; controlled Malwa, Gujarat, Bundelkhand, Delhi at times; Sikhs formed Misls; challenged Mughal power in Punjab

Jats — Suraj Mal established strong rule in Bharatpur; Rohillas powerful in Rohilkhand region; Awadh, Bengal and Hyderabad Nawabs/Nizams became independent; the Mughal Empire became a loose confederation of independent states

events.title: Nadir Shah invades and sacks Delhi
events.desc: Nadir Shah defeats the Mughals at Karnal, plunders Delhi, and carries off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.desc: The English East India Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal, marking the beginning of British political control in India.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: A decisive Company victory establishes British supremacy in North India.

events.title: Diwani rights granted
events.desc: The Mughal emperor grants the East India Company revenue-collection rights over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

events.title: Revolt of 1857 and end of Mughal rule
events.desc: Bahadur Shah II becomes a symbol of the Revolt; his deposition in 1857 and the start of British Crown rule in 1858 formally end the Mughal Empire.

people.name: Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam)
people.note: r. 1707–1712; able soldier but faced the Marathas & Sikhs.

people.name: Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela'
people.note: r. 1727–1748; cultural patronage but politically weak; reign saw Nadir Shah's invasion.

people.name: Shah Alam II
people.note: r. 1759–1806; real power lay with the Marathas, then the British.

people.name: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar)
people.note: r. 1837–1857; poet and symbol of the 1857 Revolt; deposed and exiled by the British.

prelims: Caution: do not say Mughals lost power only because of the British — internal weaknesses, economic crisis, invasions and the rise of regional powers were equally responsible
Key dates: Nadir Shah's invasion (1739), Battle of Plassey (1757), Battle of Buxar (1764), Diwani rights (1765), Revolt of 1857
mains: Analyse the decline in a holistic manner — political, economic, social, military, administrative and external factors
Legacy of the Later Mughals: preserved the idea of Indian unity and sovereignty; promoted composite culture even in decline; Bahadur Shah II became a symbol of resistance during the Revolt of 1857

periods.title: Establishment of British Power in India
periods.tagline: From Merchants to Masters — The Journey from Trade to Territorial Power
periods.overview: Tracing the English East India Company's transformation from a 1600-chartered trading company into the paramount political power in Bengal and North India: early trading privileges under Mughal farmans, rivalry with the French and Dutch, decisive battles at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), and the 1765 grant of Diwani rights that gave the Company financial control over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

phases.name: Arrival as Traders
points: East India Company established (31 December 1600); Captain William Hawkins reaches Surat (1608); English factory (trading post) at Surat (1612)

phases.name: Trading Factories & Privileges
points: Sir Thomas Roe's embassy to Jahangir's court (1615–17); Madras (Fort St. George) obtained (1639); Bombay given to the EIC by Charles II (1661, dowry of Catherine of Braganza); Calcutta (Fort William) established (1690)

phases.name: Expansion of Trade & Rivalry with Europeans
points: Farman from Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar (1717) grants major trading privileges; War of Austrian Succession — EIC vs. French begins in India (1740–48)
Rivalry with French and Dutch in Pondicherry, Chandernagore; Carnatic Wars (1746–63)

phases.name: Territorial Conquests
points: Capture of Madras by the French (1746); returned by Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748); Robert Clive becomes Military Governor of Fort St. George (1751)
Siraj-ud-Daulah captures Calcutta (Black Hole incident, 1756); Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757); Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764); Allahabad Treaty — Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar & Odisha (1765)

Key Features of Early British Expansion: Began as a trading company, not a territorial power; sought trade privileges, not immediate conquest
Took advantage of the weakness of the Mughal Empire; used diplomacy, bribery, deceit and military force

Established forts to protect trade and later as bases of power; created private armies and gradually interfered in politics; followed a policy of 'Divide and Rule'; control over the revenue system gave financial strength; defeated the French to become the chief European power
Strategies Used by the British: Diplomacy & Treaties — farmans, agreements, alliances; Divide and Rule — used internal disputes; Support to Claimants — supported one ruler against another

Bribery & Corruption — bought officials and nobles; Military Strength — well trained army, modern weapons; Economic Control — control of trade & revenue; Building Forts — bases for defence & future expansion; Intelligence Network — use of spies and information
Administrative Steps After Gaining Power: Dual System in Bengal (1765–72): Diwani (Revenue) — EIC; Nizamat (Administration) — Nawab

Appointment of Company officials as Collectors; gradual control over civil, criminal & military administration; establishment of Courts; reorganisation of revenue collection; the British became the real rulers behind the name of the Nawab

Understanding this first phase is key to understanding the complete British Empire in India

periods.title: The Sikh Empire
periods.tagline: Rise of a Powerful Indian Empire — Unity, Military Excellence & Good Governance
periods.overview: Rooted in the Sikh tradition founded by Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469) and militarised from Guru Hargobind Ji onward, the Sikh Empire is forged by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who unites the Punjabi misls, captures Lahore (1799) and is crowned Maharaja (1801). Known for religious tolerance, a modernised army and efficient administration, the empire fragments after his death (1839) into court factionalism, and is annexed by the British following the two Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49).

phases.name: Rise of Sikh Power (Background)
points: 1469: Guru Nanak Dev Ji — founder of Sikhism; 1606: Guru Hargobind Ji — militarisation begins; 1699: Khalsa Panth founded by Guru Gobind Singh Ji
1716: death of Banda Singh Bahadur; 1748: rise of the Sikh Confederacy (Misls); 1780s: rise of Sardar Ranjit Singh

phases.name: Sardar Ranjit Singh's Rise
points: 1799: Ranjit Singh captures Lahore (7 July); 1801: coronation of Ranjit Singh as Maharaja

phases.name: Capture of Lahore & Coronation
points: Conquests in Punjab & Cis-Sutlej states; 1809: Treaty of Amritsar with the British (Sutlej as boundary)

phases.name: Expansion & Conquests
points: 1813: conquest of Kangra; 1818: control over Multan; 1819: control over Kashmir; 1834: suppression of Peshawar & Hazara

phases.name: Peace & Stability, then Decline
points: 1839: death of Ranjit Singh (27 June, Lahore); decline after Ranjit Singh due to weak successors, court factions and British interference
1845–46: First Anglo-Sikh War; 1848–49: Second Anglo-Sikh War; 29 March 1849: annexation of Punjab by the British

Political Administration: Absolute monarchy under Maharaja Ranjit Singh; centralised administration with efficient officials
Divided into 3 main areas: Lahore, Multan, Peshawar (with several districts); local administration through Amils (revenue officers); village system largely unchanged — Panchayats existed
Strong intelligence network; merit-based appointments; provincial tolerance and equal treatment to all faiths
Economy: Agriculture the mainstay; canals, wells & new lands; land revenue moderate and just — no harsh exactions

Encouraged peasants and protected them from oppression; trade & commerce flourished; main exports — shawls, textiles, horses, dry fruits; major trade routes to Kabul, Central Asia, Multan, Kashmir, Sindh, etc.
Coins — Rupee (Nanakshahi) introduced; state monopolies on some goods (salt, opium etc.) to increase revenue
Military Strength: One of the most disciplined armies of India; strong cavalry, infantry and artillery; modern weapons & European training

French and Italian officers — Allard, Ventura, Court, Avitabile; famous artillery — 'Zamzama' (giant cannon); well-equipped with muskets, cannons, rockets; forts strengthened — Lahore, Attock, Multan, Peshawar, Kashmir, etc.
Religious Policy: Deeply religious but broad-minded ruler; great respect for all religions; patronised Sikhism, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism, Buddhism and Christianity

Rebuilt Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple); donated to temples, mosques, gurdwaras; employed Muslim, Hindu, Sikh officials in high positions; coined in the name of Guru Nanak Dev Ji; never forced conversion — ensured religious harmony
Caution: do not portray Ranjit Singh as a communal ruler — he was known for his religious tolerance, justice and secular administration

women.name: Mata Gujri Ji (1624–1705)
women.note: Mother of Guru Gobind Singh Ji; an epitome of courage and sacrifice; inspiration for the Khalsa.

women.name: Mai Bhago (18th century)

events.title: Death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
events.desc: His death triggers court intrigues, factionalism and weak successors, rapidly weakening the empire.

events.title: The Anglo-Sikh Wars
events.desc: Two wars against the British end in Sikh defeat; Punjab is formally annexed by the British on 29 March 1849.

people.name: Guru Gobind Singh Ji
people.note: Founded the Khalsa Panth in 1699.

Use timelines, examples and balanced analysis in answers; the Sikh Empire preserved sovereignty in North-West India against Afghan and foreign aggression
