periods.title: British Colonial Rule in India
periods.tagline: From Traders to Rulers: Conquest, Control, Exploitation & Resistance
periods.overview: The full arc of British colonial rule in India, from the political foundations laid at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) through Company rule, the 1857 Revolt and the transfer of power to the Crown (1858), the systematic economic exploitation and land revenue systems, the rise of Indian nationalism through Moderate, Extremist and Gandhian phases, and finally independence on 15 August 1947.

phases.name: Political Control & Territorial Expansion
points: Arrival of British traders (1600) leading to trading privileges & factories; political interference and military victories lead to territorial expansion

1757: Battle of Plassey — Bengal under British control; 1764: Battle of Buxar; 1773: Regulating Act — first step towards British control; 1793: Permanent Settlement; 1798–1818: Subsidiary Alliance & Expansion

phases.name: Economic Consolidation & Administrative Change
points: 1813: Charter Act — end of Company's trade monopoly; 1833: Charter Act — end of Company's commercial activities; 1835: Macaulay's Minute on Education
1857: Revolt of 1857 — First War of Independence; 1858: Government of India Act — Crown rule begins; 1861: Indian Councils Act

phases.name: Social & Cultural Changes, Rise of Nationalism
points: 1876–78: Great Famine; 1885: Formation of Indian National Congress; 1905: Partition of Bengal; 1911: capital shifted to Delhi; Bengal Partition annulled
1914–18: India's role in World War I; 1919: Rowlatt Act & Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

phases.name: Mass Movements & Transfer of Power
points: 1930: Civil Disobedience Movement; 1935: Government of India Act; 1942: Quit India Movement
1947: India gains Independence on 15 August

Economy — Exploitation & Drain of Wealth: India turned into a source of raw materials and a market for British goods; traditional industries (handloom, handicrafts) destroyed by machine-made British goods
Heavy land revenue demands extracted maximum surplus from peasants; 'Drain of Wealth' — Dadabhai Naoroji exposed economic exploitation; destruction of indigenous banking, trade and shipping
Frequent famines due to colonial policies (major famines 1770, 1876–78, 1896–97, 1899–1900); development of railways, telegraph, post, irrigation — but for imperial interests
Land Revenue Systems: Permanent Settlement (1793): Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; Zamindars as landowners
Ryotwari System — Madras, Bombay Presidency; revenue collected from cultivators
Mahalwari System — North-Western Provinces, Punjab; revenue collected from village communities
Result: exploitation of peasants, indebtedness, land alienation and rural distress
Political & Administrative System: From Company Rule to Crown Rule (1858); Governor-General → Viceroy system; centralised administration; Indian Civil Service (ICS) — steel frame of empire

District administration — Collector as key official; police, judiciary & legal system; legislative councils with limited representation; 1835 onwards — law codification (Indian Penal Code 1860, Civil Procedure Code 1859, Evidence Act 1872, etc.); Divide and Rule policy — communal & regional divisions; Princely States — indirect control through Paramountcy
Social & Cultural Impact: Introduction of Western education system (Macaulay's Minute, 1835); spread of Christianity through missionaries; social evils — sati, female infanticide, child marriage continued in many areas

Social reform movements emerged; new social classes — educated middle class, professionals, clerks; printing press & newspapers created new public opinion; Western ideas — liberty, equality, nationalism inspired leaders
Resistance & Rise of Nationalism: Early resistance: Sannyasi & Fakir Rebellion (18th c.), Poligar Rebellions (South India), Vellore Mutiny (1806), Paika Rebellion (1817), tribal revolts (Kittur, Kol, Bhil, Santhal, Munda revolts)
1857 Revolt — First War of Independence (soldiers, peasants, zamindars, rulers united); tribal revolts continued (Santhal 1855, Munda 1899, Bhil, Rampa, etc.)

Rise of nationalism in three phases: Moderate (1885–1905), Extremist (1905–1919), Gandhian Mass Phase (1919–1947); formation of the Indian National Congress (1885); ideologies of Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Swaraj

periods.title: British Administration in India
periods.tagline: From Company Rule to Crown Rule — Structure, Policies & Impact
periods.overview: A structural deep-dive into how British administration in India was actually built: from the Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784) through Company centralisation, the 1858 transfer to Crown rule, and the layered bureaucracy — Viceroy, Governor, Commissioner, Collector, Tehsildar, Village — with parallel executive, legislative and judicial structures, culminating in gradual, limited Indianisation and self-government reforms.

phases.name: Foundations of Control
points: 1773: Regulating Act — first step towards control of the EIC; Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings), Executive Council, Supreme Court at Calcutta
1784: Pitt's India Act — dual control via the Board of Control; 1793: Cornwallis Code — major administrative reforms, separation of judicial & revenue functions

phases.name: Centralisation & Company Rule
points: 1813 & 1833: Charter Acts end the Company's trade monopoly and commercial activities; 1833: Governor-General of Bengal becomes Governor-General of India (centralisation)
1835: Macaulay's Minute — English education policy; 1853: Charter Act opens Civil Services to open competitive examination (theory of merit)

phases.name: Transition to Crown Rule
points: 1857: Revolt — end of Company rule; 1858: Government of India Act — start of Crown rule, Secretary of State for India, India Council

1861: Indian Councils Act — reorganisation, Indians nominated to councils, portfolio system in provinces; 1872: financial decentralisation — provincial finance; 1882: Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution — the 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government in India'; 1892: Indian Councils Act — indirect election, limited discussion of budget

phases.name: Limited Reform & Dyarchy
points: 1909: Morley-Minto Reforms — separate electorates for Muslims, increase in councils; 1919: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — dyarchy in provinces, bicameral legislature at the Centre
1935: Government of India Act — provincial autonomy, federal structure proposed (not fully implemented); 1947: end of British rule in India

Structure of British Administration: British Crown (after 1858) → Secretary of State for India (in Britain) → India Council (advisory body) → Viceroy & Governor-General of India (representative of the Crown in India)
Executive: Governor (Provinces) → Lt. Governor/Chief Commissioner → Division → District → Sub-Division/Taluka → Village
Legislature: Imperial Legislative Council → Provincial Legislative Councils; Judiciary: Federal Court (from 1937) → High Courts → District & Subordinate Courts
ICS — The Steel Frame: Indian Civil Service (ICS) — highest administrative service; ensured unity, stability and efficiency in administration; selected through a tough competitive exam (in London till 1922, in India also after 1922 but still difficult)
High salaries, security of tenure, retirement benefits; racial bias — Indians few in number; instrument of British policy and control
Provincial Administration: Provinces governed by a Governor (later Lieutenant Governor); divided into Divisions headed by Commissioners; District headed by Collector & District Magistrate (DM) — key official for revenue, executive, judicial & police powers

Below the DM: Sub-Division (SDO)/Taluka headed by Tehsildar/Naib Tehsildar; Village — Patwari/Lambardar/Village headman; objective was efficient revenue collection, law & order and maintenance of peace
Revenue, Police & Judicial Administratio: Land revenue was the main source of government income, through Permanent Settlement (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa — Zamindars as owners), Ryotwari System (Madras, Bombay, Assam — settlement with cultivators/ryots) and Mahalwari System (North-Western Provinces, Punjab — settlement with village community)

Police Act (1861) established a modern, highly centralised police system — Superintendent of Police (SP) at district level, Thana (police station) as basic unit; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Bombay (1823), Madras (1801); High Courts established in 1862; codification of laws — Indian Penal Code (1860), Code of Civil Procedure (1859), Code of Criminal Procedure (1861), Indian Evidence Act (1872)
Local Self-Government & Reforms: Lord Ripon's Resolution (1882) — the 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government in India'; municipalities in towns, District Boards in rural areas; elected bodies with limited powers and financial dependence on government

Key reforms: Cornwallis Code (1793) — civil service reforms; Macaulay's Minute (1835) — promoted English education; Wood's Despatch (1854) — blueprint of English education in India; Hunter Commission (1882) — expansion of primary education; Montagu Declaration (1917) — pledged gradual self-government in India

periods.title: Socio-Religious Reforms During British Rule
periods.tagline: Awakening of India — Reform in Society, Renaissance of Minds
periods.overview: Nineteenth-century India's response to social evils, rigid customs and religious degeneration: a wave of reform movements — Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, Arya Samaj, Theosophical Society, Ramakrishna Mission, the Aligarh and Deoband movements, and the Singh Sabha Movement — that drew on both Western ideas of liberty, reason and humanism and India's own scriptures, aiming at social upliftment, women's rights, education, and a modern, enlightened society. These movements are widely seen as having paved the way for India's freedom struggle.

phases.name: Brahmo Samaj
points: Founder: Raja Ram Mohan Roy; monotheism, rejection of idol worship, rituals and superstitions; equality of all humans; reinterpretation of the Vedas and Upanishads

Campaigned against Sati, polygamy and caste discrimination; promoted women's rights and education; played an important role in passing the Sati Regulation (1829); later leaders — Debendranath Tagore, Keshab Chandra Sen

phases.name: Prarthana Samaj
points: Leaders: Atmaram Pandurang, M. G. Ranade; theism and devotion to one God; rejection of the caste system and social evils
Worked for the upliftment of women and lower castes; promoted inter-caste dining and marriage; leaders — M. G. Ranade, R. G. Bhandarkar, N. G. Chandavarkar

phases.name: Arya Samaj
points: Founder: Swami Dayanand Saraswati; 'Back to the Vedas'; rejection of idol worship, rituals and superstitions; equality, education, women's upliftment
Established DAV Schools and Colleges; promoted the Shuddhi Movement (re-conversion); played a role in women's education and widow remarriage; slogan: 'Krinvanto Vishwam Aryam' (Make the world noble)

phases.name: Theosophical Society & Ramakrishna Mission
points: Theosophical Society (1875) — leaders Madame H. P. Blavatsky, Henry Steel Olcott, Annie Besant; universal brotherhood of humanity; helped promote education (Central Hindu College, later BHU); Annie Besant supported the Home Rule Movement

Ramakrishna Mission (1897) — founder Swami Vivekananda (disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahansa); Practical Vedanta — service to humanity is service to God; established hospitals, schools, colleges and relief works

phases.name: Aligarh, Deoband & Singh Sabha Movements
points: Aligarh Movement (1875) — founder Sir Syed Ahmed Khan; modern education for Muslims, scientific temper; established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (later Aligarh Muslim University)
Deoband Movement (1866) — founders Maulana Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi; preservation of Islamic faith and values; established Darul Uloom, Deoband

Singh Sabha Movement (1873 onwards) — leaders Sardar Dayal Singh, Bhai Vir Singh etc.; reform and purify Sikh religion; established Khalsa Schools and Colleges; important role in the Gurdwara Reform Movement

Need for Reforms: Spread of Western education and ideas; decline of traditional values and rise of social evils; superstitions, caste discrimination, untouchability, child marriage, sati, polygamy etc.
Christian missionary criticism of Indian society and religion; print media spread new thoughts; growth of the middle class and desire for change
Features of Reform Movements: Based on humanism, rationalism and universal brotherhood; emphasis on monotheism and rejection of blind faith; fight against social evils and injustices
Promotion of women's education and upliftment; acceptance of science, modern education and reason; encouraged social service and welfare; helped build national consciousness and unity
Impact of Reform Movements: Removed social evils and encouraged social unity; improved the status of women in society; spread of education and literacy
Rise of the middle class and modern thinking; creation of public opinion and national awakening; provided moral and ideological base for the freedom struggle

periods.title: Indian Freedom Struggle
periods.tagline: A Long Struggle for Freedom, Justice & Dignity
periods.overview: From the 1857 Revolt (the First War of Independence) through four broad phases — Early/Moderate Nationalism (1885–1905), Extremism (1905–1919), the Gandhian Mass Movement phase (1919–1942) and the final Quit India phase (1942–1947) — the Indian freedom struggle united peasants, workers, students, revolutionaries and princely states in a shared demand for Purna Swaraj, ending with Independence and Partition on 15 August 1947.

phases.name: 1857 – The First War of Independence
points: Also called the Sepoy Mutiny; started 10 May 1857 at Meerut; spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Gwalior, Bareilly, Arrah etc.

Leaders: Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope, Kunwar Singh, Begum Hazrat Mahal; suppressed by 1858; impact — end of East India Company rule, Government of India Act 1858 (Crown rule began)

phases.name: Early / Moderate Nationalist Phase
points: Formation of the Indian National Congress (1885); nature: political awakening, focus on constitutional methods, reforms, representation
Prominent leaders: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta; petitions, prayers and protest as the key method

phases.name: Extremist Phase
points: Partition of Bengal (1905) sparks the Swadeshi Movement; assertive nationalism — Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Passive Resistance
Leaders: Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai; Home Rule Movement (1916, Tilak & Annie Besant); Lucknow Pact (1916); Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919)

phases.name: Gandhian Phase
points: Mass mobilisation under Mahatma Gandhi; Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918) Satyagrahas; Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22); Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34, Dandi March); Individual Satyagraha (1940–41)
Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, C. R. Das, Rajendra Prasad; participation of farmers, workers, women, students becomes nationwide

phases.name: Final Phase — Towards Freedom
points: Quit India Movement (1942) — 'Do or Die'; Indian National Army (INA) formed by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (1943); Royal Indian Navy Mutiny (Feb 1946)
Independence on 15 August 1947 and Partition of India; leaders: Subhas Chandra Bose, Jinnah, Mountbatten

Major Movements: Swadeshi Movement (1905–08) — against the Partition of Bengal; boycott of foreign goods
Home Rule Movement (1916) — led by Tilak and Annie Besant; demanded self-government
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) — boycott of foreign goods, schools, courts, titles
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34) — against the Salt Law; the famous Dandi March by Gandhi
Individual Satyagraha (1940–41) — against India's forced involvement in World War II
Quit India Movement (1942) — 'Do or Die'; demand for immediate independence
Role of Different Organisations: Indian National Congress — main platform of political struggle; Muslim League — represented Muslim interests, later demanded Pakistan; Hindu Mahasabha — promoted Hindu interests
Arya Samaj, Brahmo Samaj, Theosophical Society — social reform and national awakening; students, workers, lawyers, teachers, farmers — active participation in movements
Revolutionary Activities: Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar (Bengal); Abhinav Bharat (Maharashtra); Ghadar Party (USA & Canada)
Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) / Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA); Kakori Conspiracy (1925); Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930); Bhagat Singh and comrades' sacrifice
Tribal, Peasant & Other Contributions: Tribal revolts: Santhal (1855), Munda (Birsa Munda), Bhil, Koya, Rampa Rebellion
Peasant movements: Indigo Revolt (Bengal), Champaran Satyagraha, Kheda Satyagraha, Bardoli Satyagraha; workers' participation — mill strikes, railway workers, plantation workers
Indian National Army (INA): Formed by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose; first formed in 1942 in Southeast Asia with the help of Indian POWs; reorganized in 1943, slogan 'Chalo Dilli'
Women's Regiment — Rani Jhansi Regiment (Captain Lakshmi Sahgal); hoisted the tricolour in Andaman & Nicobar; INA trials (1945–46) united Indians and demoralized British rule

periods.title: Mahatma Gandhi
periods.tagline: Father of the Nation — Ideologue, Leader, Reformer, Nation Builder
periods.overview: A dedicated profile of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, from his early life and legal career, through his formative years fighting racial discrimination in South Africa, to the mass movements he led in India — Champaran, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India — built on his core philosophy of Satya (Truth), Ahimsa (Non-violence) and Satyagraha, until his assassination in 1948.

phases.name: Early Life & Education
points: Born 2 October 1869, Porbandar, Gujarat; parents Karamchand Gandhi (father) and Putlibai (mother)
Studied law at the Inner Temple, London (1891); went to South Africa in 1893 as a lawyer

phases.name: South Africa Years
points: Struggle against racial discrimination; development of Satyagraha as a method of resistance; his experiences of racial discrimination turned him into a satyagrahi and social reformer

phases.name: Return to India & Early Movements
points: Returned to India on 9 January 1915; joined the Indian National Movement (1915)

Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — against the indigo plantation system in Bihar, first successful satyagraha in India; Kheda Satyagraha (1918); Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918); Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), suspended after the Chauri Chaura incident

phases.name: Constructive Work & Civil Disobedience
points: Period of constructive work and social reform (1922–24); Civil Disobedience Movement & Salt Satyagraha (1930–34) — the Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) broke the Salt Law and sparked nationwide civil disobedience

phases.name: Final Years
points: Individual Satyagraha, the Wardha Scheme, rural and social work (1934–1942); Quit India Movement (1942–1947) and efforts for Hindu-Muslim unity
Assassinated in New Delhi on 30 January 1948

Core Philosophy & Principles: Truth (Satya) — Truth is God; search for truth is the goal of life; Non-violence (Ahimsa) — means of non-violence are as important as the end
Satyagraha — truth-force or soul-force; resistance through love and non-violence; Sarvodaya — welfare of all, upliftment of the last person

Swaraj — self-rule, self-control at individual and national level; Swadeshi — use of indigenous goods, economic self-reliance; Trusteeship — the wealthy are trustees of their wealth for society; Constructive Programme — education, hygiene, village industries, removal of untouchability
Major Movements Led: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — against the indigo plantation system; first successful satyagraha in India
Kheda Satyagraha (1918) — for peasants of Gujarat against high land revenue; partial tax relief granted
Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) — for fair wages of textile workers; workers' demand accepted
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) — boycott of British institutions, titles, foreign goods; suspended after Chauri Chaura
Salt Satyagraha / Civil Disobedience (1930) — Dandi March broke the Salt Law, sparked nationwide civil disobedience
Round Table Conferences (1930–32) — participated in all three London conferences
Individual Satyagraha (1940–41) — protest against India's involvement in World War II
Quit India Movement (1942) — 'Do or Die' call for immediate end of British rule
Role in Socio-Religious Reforms: Fought against untouchability; called Dalits 'Harijans' (children of God); worked for their upliftment through the Harijan Sevak Sangh
Promoted communal harmony; worked with all religions; advocated basic education (Nai Talim); emphasized cleanliness, hygiene, prohibition
Encouraged simple living, removal of caste barriers, women's upliftment; started journals: Young India, Harijan, Navajivan

periods.title: Independence of India
periods.tagline: The Final Phase of the Freedom Struggle — From War to Independence
periods.overview: A close-focus account of the last, decisive eight years of the freedom struggle: India's involuntary entry into World War II, the failed British offers (August Offer, Cripps Mission, Wavell Plan, Cabinet Mission), the Quit India Movement, the Indian National Army, communal politics and the Lahore Resolution, and the final Mountbatten Plan that delivered both independence and the partition of India on 15 August 1947.

phases.name: War & Political Deadlock
points: 3 September 1939: World War II begins; India declared a belligerent without consulting Indian leaders; Congress ministries in 8 provinces resign in protest
August Offer (1940): British offer of constitutional advance; Individual Satyagraha launched by Gandhi (1st Satyagrahi — Vinoba Bhave)

phases.name: Missions & Mass Movement
points: Cripps Mission comes to India (March 1942); Quit India Movement launched (8 August 1942, Bombay, Gowalia Tank Maidan)
Provisional Government of Azad Hind (INA) announced in Singapore (October 1943)

phases.name: Endgame of the War
points: INA advances from Imphal-Kohima but is forced to retreat (March–July 1944); Wavell Plan announced (June 1945); Simla Conference (June–July 1945)

phases.name: Transfer of Power
points: Cabinet Mission comes to India (March–June 1946); Direct Action Day by the Muslim League (16 August 1946); Interim Government formed (2 September 1946)

Mountbatten Plan announced (3 June 1947); Indian Independence Act passed by British Parliament (18 July 1947); India becomes independent (15 August 1947); Partition of India — creation of India and Pakistan

Major Political Developments: Congress demanded complete independence and a united India; Muslim League under Jinnah demanded Pakistan; British used divide and rule, negotiations, missions and plans

Political demands changed over time: from Complete Independence (1939–40) to acceptance of Partition (Mountbatten Plan, 1947); Congress moved from complete independence to transfer of power immediately, while the League moved from safeguards for Muslims to demanding Pakistan
Major British Initiatives & Missions: August Offer (1940) — to secure Indian support in WWII; promised Dominion status after the war; rejected by Congress & League
Cripps Mission (1942) — to gain Indian cooperation; offered Dominion status after the war and the right of provinces to opt out; rejected as 'a post-dated cheque'

Wavell Plan (1945) — to break the deadlock and form an Executive Council; reconstitution of the Viceroy's Council with equal representation of Indians & Muslims; Simla Conference failed due to the League's veto

Cabinet Mission (1946) — to frame a constitution & transfer power; proposed a Union of India with 3 groups, a Constituent Assembly and an Interim Government; initially accepted but differences later emerged
Mountbatten Plan (1947) — to transfer power quickly; partition of India, creation of India & Pakistan; accepted as the only practical solution
The INA & the Role of Mahatma Gandhi: INA: leader Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose; first formed by Capt. Mohan Singh (1942), reorganised by Netaji (1943); Azad Hind Government proclaimed 21 October 1943 in Singapore; Rani of Jhansi Regiment (all women, led by Captain Lakshmi Sahgal); INA Trials (1945–46) generated nationwide sympathy and weakened British loyalty in the armed forces

Gandhi favoured non-violent mass struggle; demanded freedom before cooperation during WWII; launched Individual Satyagraha (1940); led the Quit India Movement (1942); emphasised Hindu-Muslim unity and removal of untouchability
Communal Politics & Partition: 1940 Lahore Resolution — Muslim League demanded 'independent states' for Muslims; growth of communal politics; the two-nation theory emphasised

Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) — large-scale communal violence; Cabinet Mission failed due to differences on Grouping and Partition; Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) — Partition accepted; led to massive displacement, violence and loss of life

periods.title: Independent India — Major Phases
periods.tagline: A Journey of Nation-Building, Development & Democracy
periods.overview: Independent India's story organised into five broad phases — Nation-Building & Consolidation (1947–1964), Stabilization & Challenges (1965–1977), Reassessment & Reforms Initiation (1977–1991), Liberalisation & Economic Reforms (1991–2014), and New India (2014–Present) — tracing the journey from a newly independent, divided nation to the world's largest democracy pursuing global leadership and 'Viksit Bharat' by 2047. Each phase is explored in full depth on its own dedicated decade page.

phases.name: Nation-Building & Consolidation
points: Integration of over 560 Princely States (Sardar Patel & V. P. Menon); Constitution adopted 26 November 1949, came into force 26 January 1950; First General Elections (1951–52, universal adult franchise)
Five Year Plans begin; Non-Aligned Movement & Panchsheel principles; Linguistic Reorganisation of States (1956); scientific temper — IITs, AIIMS, CSIR, DRDO founded

phases.name: Stabilization & Challenges
points: Wars: 1965 (Pakistan), 1971 (Bangladesh Liberation); Green Revolution — self-sufficiency in food grains; Bank Nationalisation (1969); abolition of Privy Purses (1971)
Garibi Hatao — focus on poverty alleviation; Emergency (1975–77) — civil liberties suspended; beginning of India's nuclear programme (Pokhran-I, 1974)

phases.name: Reassessment & Reforms Initiation
points: Janata Party government (1977–79) — end of Congress dominance; 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) strengthened democracy; rise of regional parties & coalition politics
Technology Missions — telecom, literacy; economic reforms initiated slowly (delicensing, MRTP Act relaxation); insurgencies in Punjab, Assam, Kashmir, Northeast; Balance of Payments crisis (1990–91)

phases.name: Liberalisation & Economic Reforms
points: New Economic Policy (1991) — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation; high GDP growth, rise of the middle class

IT & services revolution — Bangalore, Hyderabad etc.; infrastructure development — roads, ports, telecom; key laws — RTI Act (2005), RTE Act (2009); social welfare — MNREGA (2005), Food Security Act (2013); coalition-era politics with reform continuity

phases.name: New India — Transformation & Aspirations
points: Vision — Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas; Digital India, Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile (JAM Trinity); Swachh Bharat Mission, PM Awas Yojana
Ujjwala Yojana, Ayushman Bharat; Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan (2020); infrastructure push — Bharatmala, Sagarmala; India's rise on the global stage — G20, Climate Leadership

Major Achievements: Democracy — world's largest democracy; Unity & Integrity — integration of states, strong federal structure; Economic Development — from a low-income to an emerging economy

Agricultural Growth — food self-sufficiency; Science & Technology — space, nuclear, IT, pharma; Social Progress — education, health, gender empowerment; Global Standing — peacekeeping, NAM, G20, Yoga & culture; Infrastructure — roads, railways, ports, digital
Challenges Faced: Poverty, unemployment, inequality; communalism, regionalism & terrorism; corruption & political instability
Environmental degradation; population pressure & urbanisation; education, health & human development gaps
Institutions That Shaped India: Parliament & Judiciary; Election Commission; Indian Administrative Service; Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog); Reserve Bank of India; Public Sector Undertakings; Universities & Research Institutions; Armed Forces

periods.title: India After Independence (1947–1964)
periods.tagline: From Freedom to Nation-Building
periods.overview: The foundational years of the Republic: Partition and the integration of over 560 princely states, the framing and adoption of the Constitution (1950), the beginning of Five-Year Plans and Non-Alignment, linguistic reorganisation of states (1956), the 1962 Sino-Indian War, and Nehru's death in 1964 — laying the foundation of India as a sovereign, democratic, secular, socialist republic.

phases.name: Independence & Integration
points: 15 August 1947: Independence; Partition of British India; Jawaharlal Nehru becomes Prime Minister; Kashmir crisis begins
30 January 1948: Mahatma Gandhi assassinated; 1948: Hyderabad Police Action (Operation Polo), Junagadh integration; 1949: Constitution adopted (26 November)

phases.name: The Republic Begins
points: 26 January 1950: Constitution comes into force; Dr. Rajendra Prasad becomes first President; Planning Commission established; Supreme Court established
1951: First Five-Year Plan launched; 1952: First General Elections, universal adult franchise; 1953: Andhra State created (linguistic reorganisation begins)

phases.name: Foreign Policy & Reorganisation
points: 1954: Panchsheel Agreement with China; 1955: Bandung Conference — Afro-Asian solidarity, Second Five-Year Plan; 1956: States Reorganisation Act — linguistic reorganisation of states
1957: Second General Elections; Communist government elected in Kerala (first democratically elected communist government in the world)

phases.name: Border Tensions & Consolidation
points: 1958: AFSPA enacted for disturbed areas; 1959: Dalai Lama arrives in India after leaving Tibet; India-China tensions intensify; 1960: Indus Waters Treaty between India & Pakistan
1961: Goa Liberation / annexation of Goa, Daman & Diu integrated into India

phases.name: War & Transition

Constitution of India — Key Features: Written & detailed Constitution; then the longest in the world; federal with a unitary bias; Parliamentary System; Fundamental Rights; Directive Principles of State Policy
Independent Judiciary; Universal Adult Franchise; single citizenship; secular state; equality before law
Foreign Policy & Non-Alignment: Panchsheel (1954); Bandung Conference (1955); Non-Aligned Movement (NAM); anti-colonialism and support to liberation movements; non-alignment as a 'third alternative' during the Cold War
Five-Year Plans: First Plan (1951–56): agriculture, irrigation, community development, rehabilitation; Harrod-Domar growth model
Second Plan (1956–61): heavy industry, machine building, public sector; Mahalanobis model
Third Plan (1961–66): self-reliance, agriculture, education, defence, infrastructure; slowdown due to 1962 war
Wars & Security: 1947–48: First India-Pakistan War (over Kashmir); 1962: Sino-Indian War (NEFA & Ladakh); impact — defence reorganisation, increase in defence spending, strategic realism emerges
Social Reforms & Transformation: Abolition of untouchability (Article 17); Hindu Code Bills (1955–56) — reforms in marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption; Maternity Benefit Act (1961); Community Development Programme (1952); Cooperative Movement; literacy campaigns, tribal welfare initiatives; refugee rehabilitation and urban resettlement

periods.title: India After Independence (1965–1980)
periods.tagline: From Nation-Building to National Strength
periods.overview: A period of wars and consolidation of national strength: the 1965 and 1971 wars with Pakistan (the latter creating Bangladesh), the Green Revolution's transformation of Indian agriculture, Bank Nationalisation, the controversial Emergency (1975–77) and its aftermath, and India's first nuclear test (Pokhran-I, 1974), ending with the fall of the Janata government and Indira Gandhi's return to power in 1980.

phases.name: War & Political Change
points: 1965: Indo-Pak War (Sept); Tashkent Agreement (Jan 1966); Lal Bahadur Shastri dies (11 Jan 1966); Indira Gandhi becomes Prime Minister

1966: Green Revolution begins (Punjab, Haryana, Western UP); 1967: Fourth General Elections, Congress loses in several states; Naxalbari Movement begins in West Bengal; 1968: crop production increases

phases.name: Bank Nationalisation & Growth
points: 1969: 14 major banks nationalised; Congress split (Congress-O and Congress-R); Garibi Hatao slogan; 1970: growth in steel, coal, heavy industries, 20-Point Economic Programme

1971: Indo-Pak War (Dec) — Bangladesh Liberation War, 93,000 Pakistani soldiers surrender, creation of Bangladesh, Shimla Agreement (July); 1972: reorganisation of North-Eastern states, Mizoram made a Union Territory

phases.name: Oil Crisis & Nuclear Test
points: 1973: Oil Crisis — rise in petroleum prices, impact on economy, food grain imports increase; 1974: Pokhran-I Nuclear Test (18 May), Railway Strike (May), Bihar Movement / JP Movement begins
1975: Allahabad High Court verdict against the PM (12 June); Emergency declared (25 June); press censorship, 20-Point Programme, political opposition arrested, forceful sterilisation campaign

phases.name: The Emergency & Its Aftermath
points: 1976: 42nd Constitutional Amendment — Fundamental Duties added, 'Socialist' and 'Secular' added to the Preamble; 1977: Emergency withdrawn (Jan), General Elections (March), Janata Party victory, first non-Congress government at the Centre, Morarji Desai becomes PM
1978: 44th Constitutional Amendment — restoration of civil liberties, end of arbitrary arrests, Janata government internal differences

Political & Constitutional Developments: Strengthening of institutions and parliamentary democracy; Election Commission gains credibility; judiciary asserts independence
Constitutional amendments: 24th, 25th, 42nd (1976), 44th (1978); rise of regional assertion and coalition politics
Economic Development & Planning: Third Plan (1961–66): self-reliance, agriculture, education, industry; Plan Holiday (1966–69): economic stabilisation; Fourth Plan (1969–74): growth with stability and self-reliance; Fifth Plan (1974–79): poverty removal (Garibi Hatao)

Key features: Green Revolution boosts food grain production; Bank Nationalisation (1969); expansion of public sector undertakings; poverty remains a major challenge; inflation, oil crisis & fiscal deficits
Foreign Policy & International Relations: Non-Aligned Movement leadership continues; Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (1971); support to liberation movements; strong stand on disarmament and global peace

Key events: Tashkent Agreement (1965) with Pakistan; Shimla Agreement (1971) with Pakistan; creation of Bangladesh (1971); strong global support after Pokhran-I (1974); Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979) — India maintains a balanced approach
Science, Technology & National Achieveme: Pokhran-I Nuclear Test (1974); launch of Aryabhata, India's first satellite (1975); growth in space and atomic energy programmes; development in agriculture — HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation; White Revolution (Operation Flood begins, 1970); expansion of telecom and broadcasting

periods.title: The French Revolution
periods.tagline: The Birth of Modern Politics — Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
periods.overview: A global-context deep-dive (companion to the World History chart) on the revolution that overthrew absolute monarchy in France and helped define the ideals of modern democracy. Moving through three phases — Monarchy in Crisis, Republic & Radicalisation, and the Directory — it traces the fall of the Bastille, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the execution of Louis XVI, the Reign of Terror, and the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte, whose 1799 coup ends the revolutionary decade.

phases.name: Phase I — Monarchy in Crisis
points: 1787–88: financial crisis deepens, calls for the Estates General; 5 May 1789: Estates General meets at Versailles

17 June 1789: the Third Estate declares itself the National Assembly; 20 June 1789: Tennis Court Oath — vow not to disperse until France has a Constitution; 14 July 1789: Storming of the Bastille — symbol of royal tyranny
4 August 1789: Abolition of Feudalism; 26 August 1789: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; 1791: Constitution of 1791 establishes a Constitutional Monarchy

phases.name: Phase II — Republic & Radicalisation
points: 10 August 1792: Storming of the Tuileries, the monarchy suspended; 21 September 1792: France declared a Republic
21 January 1793: Execution of Louis XVI; Jacobin control begins; 1793–94: Reign of Terror under Robespierre; 27 July 1794: Fall of Robespierre

phases.name: Phase III — Directory & End of Revolution
points: 1795: Directory Constitution — rule of Five Directors; 1799: Coup of 18 Brumaire by Napoleon Bonaparte (9 November); end of the Revolution

Causes of the Revolution: Political: absolute monarchy of Louis XVI, arbitrary rule with no popular participation, influence of Enlightenment thinkers
Social: society divided into Three Estates, privileges enjoyed by Clergy & Nobility, the burden of taxes fell on the Third Estate

Economic: financial crisis due to wars (including support for the American Revolution), extravagant royal expenditure, inefficient tax system and heavy debts, poor harvests in the 1780s leading to famine and hunger
Intellectual: Enlightenment ideas of Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Diderot; ideas of liberty, equality, the Social Contract and popular sovereignty
The Three Estates: First Estate — Clergy (0.5%): owned 10% of land, paid little or no tax
Second Estate — Nobility (1.5%): owned 20% of land, exempted from most taxes
Third Estate (97%): bourgeoisie, professionals, peasants, workers; paid heavy taxes, owned little land, had no political power
The Reign of Terror (1793–94): Why: war with European powers, internal revolts, economic crisis, counter-revolutionary threats, the perceived need to 'save the revolution'
Features: Committee of Public Safety formed, the Law of Suspects, a Revolutionary Tribunal, use of the guillotine, thousands executed
Impact: suppressed enemies of the revolution, created fear and instability, but also saved the revolution from collapse
Consequences of the Revolution: Political: end of absolute monarchy; rise of the nation-state; spread of democratic ideas; constitutionalism and rule of law
Social: abolition of feudalism; equality before law; end of the privileges of Church & Nobility; rise of the middle class
Economic: abolition of feudal dues; redistribution of Church lands; encouraged capitalism and free trade
Ideological & Cultural: spread of ideas of Liberty, Equality, Fraternity; inspired nationalist movements in Europe; secularism and rational thinking; birth of modern citizenship and democracy

periods.title: World War I
periods.tagline: The Great War — Complete Timeline & Flow
periods.overview: A global-context deep-dive on the war that began with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and, through a chain reaction of alliances, engulfed Europe and the world. Covers the long-term causes (nationalism, imperialism, militarism, the alliance system, the Balkan crisis), major battles, India's large-scale but often under-recognised contribution, the Russian Revolution's exit from the war, the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations, and the unresolved grievances that would lead directly to World War II.

phases.name: Outbreak
points: 28 June 1914: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo — the spark; Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia; Russia mobilises
Germany declares war on Russia, then on France; German invasion of Belgium; Britain enters the war; the European war becomes a World War

phases.name: Trench Warfare & Total War
points: 1914–15: Trench warfare develops, characterised by new weapons and total mobilisation of resources; 1915–16: 'Total War' — economic, industrial and global mobilisation
1917: Russian Revolution (February & October); Russia withdraws from the war (Treaty of Brest-Litovsk); 1917–18: USA enters the war (April 1917) — a turning point

phases.name: End of the War
points: 1918: Central Powers collapse; Armistice signed on 11 November 1918; 1919: Treaty of Versailles signed (28 June)

phases.name: Aftermath
points: League of Nations established (1920) as part of the peace settlement; a new (but unstable) world order emerges, with unresolved grievances — especially Germany's — that lay the path to World War II

Long-Term Causes (The Big Five): Nationalism: German nationalism, French revanchism after the Franco-Prussian War, Pan-Slavism, Serbian nationalism, aspirations of subject peoples in the multi-national Austro-Hungarian Empire
Imperialism: competition for colonies, rivalry over Africa and Asia, Anglo-German competition, French-German rivalry, colonial prestige
Militarism: arms race, naval rivalry, German naval expansion challenging British naval supremacy, military planning, conscription, influence of military elites
Alliance System: the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente, secret diplomacy, the security dilemma, balance-of-power politics
Balkan Crisis: decline of Ottoman authority, Balkan nationalism, Serbian expansion, Austro-Hungarian fear of Serbian nationalism, Russian support for Slavic peoples, and the Balkan Wars (1912–13)
The Alliance System: Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy (Italy later switched sides and joined the Allies in 1915)
Triple Entente: Britain, France, Russia; the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria later joined the Central Powers; Japan and eventually the USA (1917) joined the Allies
The alliance system converted a regional Balkan crisis into a continental, and eventually global, war
India's Contribution: Over 13 lakh Indian soldiers served overseas; fought in Flanders, Gallipoli, Mesopotamia and East Africa; total casualties — around 74,000
Economic & material support: war loans, taxes, donations; supply of food, raw materials and war stores; Indian industries expanded, causing a heavy economic burden at home
Political impact on India: rise of national consciousness; demand for greater self-government; the Montagu Declaration (1917) and the strengthened freedom movement
Consequences of the War: Political: end of empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, Russian); creation of new nations; rise of democracy; formation of the League of Nations
Economic: massive destruction; heavy war debts; war reparations; inflation and economic instability
Social: huge loss of life (roughly 1 crore/10 million dead); wounded soldiers; displaced populations; psychological trauma
Women's role: women entered the workforce in large numbers; worked in factories, offices and farms; the demand for equal rights intensified

periods.title: The Russian Revolution
periods.tagline: The Birth of the World's First Socialist State
periods.overview: A global-context deep-dive on 1917's twin revolutions — the February Revolution that toppled the Tsarist autocracy after 300 years of Romanov rule, and the Bolshevik-led October Revolution that established the world's first socialist state under the slogan 'Peace, Bread and Land'. Traces the causes, the period of Dual Power, the October seizure of power, the Russian Civil War between Reds and Whites, War Communism and the New Economic Policy, and the eventual formation of the USSR (1922).

phases.name: Causes & Build-Up
points: 1894–1905: unrest, strikes, rise of socialist ideas; 1905: Revolution of 1905, 'Bloody Sunday'; 1905–14: Stolypin Reforms, limited changes
1914: Russia enters World War I; 1915–16: war hardships increase — food shortages, military defeats, economic strain

phases.name: February Revolution
points: Food shortages, long working hours and war-related misery; strikes and demonstrations in Petrograd (23 Feb / 8 March 1917); soldiers join the protest
The Duma forms a Provisional Committee; Tsar Nicholas II abdicates on 2 March 1917; result — end of 300 years of Romanov dynasty and Tsarist autocracy

phases.name: Dual Power
points: Two centres of power emerge: the Provisional Government (bourgeois/liberals) and the Soviets (Councils of Workers, Soldiers & Peasants)

Lenin returns to Russia (April 1917); the Provisional Government continues the war and fails to solve the problems of bread, land and peace; the Soviets gain growing support, creating the conditions for a Bolshevik takeover

phases.name: October Revolution
points: Bolsheviks, under a Military Revolutionary Committee led by Trotsky, seize key points in Petrograd; the Winter Palace is captured; the Provisional Government is overthrown
The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets endorses the Bolshevik takeover; Soviet power is established; Decree on Peace and Decree on Land issued (Nov 1917)

phases.name: Civil War & Consolidation
points: 1918–1921: Russian Civil War between the Red Army (Bolsheviks) and the White Army (anti-Bolsheviks, backed by foreign powers)
1921: New Economic Policy (NEP) introduced by Lenin; 30 December 1922: Formation of the USSR; 1924: Lenin dies; 1927 onwards: rise of Stalin and consolidation of the USSR

Causes of the Revolution: Political: autocratic rule of the Tsars, absence of democracy and fundamental rights, repression, censorship and the secret police (Okhrana)
Social: rigid social hierarchy, oppression of peasants and workers, influence of socialist and Marxist ideas
Economic: a backward, feudal economy, industrial backwardness, exploitation of workers, poor living conditions, unequal distribution of land
Immediate cause: defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) and participation in World War I (1914–17) which brought food shortages, inflation and unemployment
Important Decrees & Early Measures: Decree on Peace (Nov 1917) — offered immediate peace without annexations or indemnities; Decree on Land (Nov 1917) — abolished private ownership of land, land to be used by those who work it

Other measures: 8-hour working day, workers' control in factories, nationalisation of banks, abolition of Tsarist titles, control over press & education, equality of all nationalities, formation of the Cheka (secret police)
War Communism vs New Economic Policy (NE: War Communism (1918–21): nationalisation of industries, grain requisition from peasants, ban on private trade, rationing — aimed to support the war effort but led to economic collapse and peasant discontent (e.g. the Kronstadt Rebellion, 1921)

New Economic Policy (1921): introduced by Lenin; partial restoration of private trade; small-scale private industry allowed; tax in kind instead of requisition; aimed to revive the economy and win back the support of peasants — resulted in economic recovery and stability
Consequences of the Russian Revolution: Political: end of Tsarist autocracy; establishment of a Communist State; a one-party system; centralised authority
Social: equality in theory; women gained rights; education expanded; class distinctions challenged
Economic: nationalisation of industries; land redistributed; a planned economy; industrialisation later under Five-Year Plans

International: inspired revolutions worldwide; founding of the Communist International (Comintern) in 1919; led to ideological conflicts of Capitalism vs Communism that shaped the 20th century, including the Cold War

periods.title: World War II
periods.tagline: The Second World War — Complete Timeline & Flow
periods.overview: A global-context deep-dive on history's deadliest conflict: the rise of aggressive dictatorships and the failure of appeasement, the German invasion of Poland (1939), the war's spread across European and Pacific theatres, the Holocaust, India's massive military and economic contribution, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan's surrender, and the war's direct consequences — the United Nations, decolonisation, and the Cold War.

phases.name: Outbreak
points: 1 September 1939: Germany invades Poland; 3 September 1939: Britain and France declare war on Germany; September 1939 – April 1940: the 'Phoney War'

phases.name: German Blitzkrieg & Battle of Britain
points: April–June 1940: German Blitzkrieg across Europe — Denmark, Norway, Netherlands, Belgium, France; June 1940: Fall of France; July–October 1940: Battle of Britain — first major Axis defeat

phases.name: The War Becomes Global
points: 22 June 1941: Germany invades the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa); 7 December 1941: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; 8 December 1941: USA declares war on Japan; the war becomes truly global

phases.name: Turning Points
points: 1942: Allies check Axis advance at El Alamein and Midway; February 1943: surrender of German forces at Stalingrad — major turning point on the Eastern Front; 1943–45: Allied advance in Europe and the Pacific

phases.name: Allied Victory
points: 6 June 1944: D-Day — Allied invasion of Normandy, opening a second front; April 1945: Allies cross the Rhine; 8 May 1945: Germany surrenders (VE Day)
6 & 9 August 1945: Atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; 15 August 1945: Japan surrenders; 2 September 1945: formal end of World War II (VJ Day)

Long-Term Causes (The Big Five): Aggressive Nationalism: extreme nationalism in Germany, Italy and Japan; revanchism in Germany after the Treaty of Versailles
Imperialism: quest for colonies, resources and markets; Japanese expansionism in Asia; Italian ambitions in Africa and the Mediterranean
Militarism: glorification of military power, arms race, large standing armies and conscription
Economic Factors: the Great Depression (1929) led to economic hardship, unemployment and political instability
Failure of Collective Security: the League of Nations failed to act; the policy of Appeasement encouraged aggressors
Appeasement Policy: Britain and France tried to avoid war by making concessions to Hitler: 1936 — Remilitarisation of the Rhineland (no action taken); 1938 — Anschluss with Austria (no action taken); 1938 — Munich Agreement over the Sudetenland (no action taken); this ultimately encouraged Hitler's further aggression
India's Contribution in World War II: Indian Forces: over 25 lakh Indian soldiers served overseas — among the largest volunteer forces in history; fought in Europe, North Africa, West Asia, South East Asia; important battles — El Alamein, Monte Cassino, Imphal, Burma; the Indian Air Force and Indian Navy also played significant roles

Economic & Industrial: the war boosted Indian industries; production of arms, ammunition, vehicles, uniforms; development of infrastructure (roads, ports, airfields); inflation and famine (Bengal Famine, 1943) had a severe negative impact

Political impact: rise of the demand for freedom; the Indian National Army (INA), led by Subhas Chandra Bose, fought alongside Axis forces against the British; the Quit India Movement (1942) unfolds during the war
The Holocaust: Nazi Germany persecuted and murdered Jews and other minorities; six million Jews were murdered in concentration camps; major camps included Auschwitz, Treblinka, Dachau, Buchenwald — one of the darkest chapters in human history
Consequences of World War II: Political: decline of Europe as a world power; rise of the USA and Soviet Union as superpowers; the decolonisation movement gains momentum; establishment of the United Nations; beginning of the Cold War
Economic: massive destruction of life and property; heavy war debts; the Marshall Plan by the USA for Europe's recovery; economic rise of the USA
Social: loss of millions of lives (6 to 7 crore); displacement of populations; advancement in science and technology; women's role increased in the workforce
Moral: awareness of human rights grows; atrocities like the Holocaust shock the world; recognition of the need for world peace and cooperation
